en: Aśvaghoṣa: *Buddhacarita*—There was a king named Śuddhodana, of the Ikṣvāku lineage, possessing the majesty of the Ikṣvākus; among the Śākyas, he was of unblemished conduct and, like the autumn moon, beloved by his subjects. (Bc 1.1)
That king, who was like Indra, had a wife whose splendor and power were equal to his own;
she was named Māyā, peerless and illusory in nature, like Lakṣmī upon a lotus or the steadfast Earth itself.
The king lived with her, never even thinking of the splendor of Vaiśravaṇa;
then, like a goddess endowed with meditative concentration, she conceived a child, being free from all evil.
Before she had conceived a child, the queen of the lord of men saw in a dream a single white king of elephants entering her own body; on account of that, she did not experience any distress.
Carrying the glory of her lineage within her womb as the queen of that god-like king, she experienced neither fatigue nor sorrow nor delusion; yet she secretly longed to go to the forest.
He sought out that forest region named Lumbinī— a land of variegated trees as delightful as Caitraratha,
secluded and conducive to meditation— and spoke to the king, desiring to dwell there.

Perceiving that she possessed a noble disposition and was inclined toward the Dharma, the lord of the earth— filled with curiosity and joy— departed from the auspicious city for her sake, and not for the purpose of visiting a monastery.
In that glorious grove, the queen, perceiving that the time of delivery had arrived,
took her place upon a couch covered with a canopy, while being greeted with joy by thousands of women.
Then the constellation Puṣya became favorable for that queen, who was consecrated by her vow;
from her side a son was born for the welfare of the world, without pain and free from ailment.
Just as [the birth] of Aurva was from the thigh, that of Pṛthu from the hand, that of Māndhātṛ— who was equal to Indra— from the head,
and that of Kakṣīvat from the shoulder region, even so was his birth.
Gradually emerging from the womb, he shone like one fallen from the sky who was not born from a birth canal;
for throughout many eons he had cultivated his self, and thus he was born with full awareness, not deluded.
He who shone with brilliance and composure like the young sun descended upon the earth,
though so intensely radiant, captivated the eyes of all who gazed upon him as does the moon.
For with the radiance of his own limbs blazing forth, he eclipsed the light of the lamps like the sun;
possessing the beautiful hue of precious Jāmbūnada gold, he illuminated all the directions.
With steps that were unhurried, upright, and raised high, yet possessed of a long-striding gait like a crushing force,
he, resembling the constellation of the Seven Sages, took seven firm strides.

"I am born for enlightenment for the sake of the welfare of the world; this is my final birth in existence," he said, looking toward the four quarters with the gait of a lion, and uttered these words which bring about the welfare of those capable of liberation.
Two streams of water, as white as moonbeams, flowing from the sky— one with a cool potency and the other with a warm potency—
fell upon his gentle head to provide the pleasure of contact with his body.
He was reclining on a bed with a magnificent canopy and limbs radiant with gold, its feet made of lapis lazuli;
out of reverence for him, the lords of the yakṣas stood surrounding him, holding golden lotuses in their hands.
And by his power, the invisible denizens of heaven in the sky, bowing their heads,
held a white parasol over him and uttered supreme benedictions for his enlightenment.
The mahoragas, out of their thirst for the excellence of the Dharma and having performed services under past Buddhas,
fanned him with yak-tail whisks, their eyes distinguished by devotion, and scattered mandārava flowers over him.

Delighted by the virtue of the Tathāgata’s appearance, the Śuddhāvāsa deities and those of pure essence rejoiced—even though their own passion had departed—for the sake of the world submerged in suffering. (Bc 1.20)
At his birth, the earth, pinned down by the king of mountains, shook like a boat struck by the wind;
and a rain scented with sandalwood and filled with blue and red lotuses fell from a cloudless sky.
Breezes blew, pleasant to the touch and delightful, casting down celestial garments;
the sun shone with even greater brilliance, and the fire blazed with gentle flames, though unfanned.
And in the north-eastern part of the dwelling, a well with pure white water appeared spontaneously,
into which the women of the inner apartments, filled with wonder, performed their rites as if at a sacred bathing place.
The forest was filled with hosts of divine beings seeking the Dharma who had gathered to behold him;
out of sheer curiosity, they even caused flowers to fall from the trees, though it was not the season for them.
Abandoned by unwholesome spirits who had ceased their violence, he caused no suffering among his own followers or others;
indeed, all diseases of men in the world were pacified without any effort.
The beasts and birds raised a sweet cry, and the rivers became calm as their waters flowed;
the quarters of the sky grew clear, and in a cloudless, stainless firmament, celestial drums resounded.
When the Teacher was born for the sake of the world’s liberation, the disordered universe attained tranquility;
indeed, as if having found a wise protector, Māra alone did not find joy in the world.
Beholding his divine and marvelous birth, even the steadfast king was moved to great agitation;
out of affection, that lord of men shed two streams of water born of both fear and joy.
Having heard of his superhuman power, the queen— whose heart was by nature moist with compassion—
became both joyful and afraid, like a stream of water consisting of a mixture of cold and heat.
Gazing upon that very cause of fear, the grown women were unable even to meditate;
yet, being purified, they performed auspicious rites and entreated the hosts of gods for the welfare of the infant.
And the brahmins, renowned for their learning, character, and eloquence, having heard the omens and deliberated upon them thoroughly,
approached the king— whose face was blooming yet startled and radiant— and spoke to him with a mixture of fear and serenity.
Those beings who exist on earth and desire peace do not seek even a single quality in a son;
yet this son of yours exists as the lamp of your lineage.
Therefore, O King, celebrate a festival of dance today!
Abandoning anxiety, be peaceful in mind and rejoice; your lineage shall partake in increase.
This leader of the world, who has become like a son to you, is the protector of those afflicted by suffering upon this earth.
This Dīpaprabha, whose body shines like gold and who is endowed with auspicious marks, is a treasure-house of virtues;
in due time, he will attain the state of a Buddha-sage or supreme glory.
If he should desire the glory of the entire earth, having conquered it through righteousness,
he would shine among kings as the radiant sun shines among all the planets.
Or else, for the sake of liberation, he should go to the forest;
having truly and completely conquered all the doctrines on earth that have been highly esteemed, he would shine like Mount Sumeru among the mountains.

Just as gold is pure amidst its ore, Meru among mountains, the ocean among bodies of water, the moon among stars, and the sun among those that give heat, so too are you, O son, the most excellent among bipeds.
His eyes were unblinking, wide, moist, radiant, and likewise clear;
with their steady, long, black, and pure lashes, they were indeed capable of beholding all phenomena.
"For what reason does the prince possess these excellent qualities described by you, which neither the sages nor the kings of old attained? Thus questioned, the twice-born spoke to him.
Renowned deeds, fame, and wisdom do not exist first and come into being later;
rather, all virtues arise from a cause. Understand here our illustrations of this.
O gentle one, that treatise on statecraft which the two seers Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras— the progenitors of their lineages— did not compose,
was created by their sons, Śukra and Bṛhaspati, in the course of time.
Sārasvata also proclaimed the lost Veda, which those of old had not seen;
likewise Vyāsa divided it into many parts, which Vasiṣṭha, being powerless, had not done.
Vālmīki first produced poetry, which the great seer Cyavana did not compose;
and that medical science which Atri did not create was later proclaimed by the seer Ātreya.
O King, that state of being twice-born which Kuśika did not obtain was attained by Gādhi’s son;
and Sagara established the boundary at the ocean which the Ikṣvākus had not previously fixed.
Janaka attained the status of a teacher in the practice of yoga— a position unattained by other twice-borns—
and as for those celebrated deeds of Śauri, Śūra and the others were powerless to perform them.
Therefore, neither age nor lineage serves as a criterion for superiority anywhere in the world;
for among kings and sages, various deeds were accomplished by sons that had not been performed by their ancestors.
Thus consoled and cheered by those trustworthy brahmins,
the king cast away his unwelcome apprehension from his mind and ascended to even greater joy.
And being pleased with those best of the twice-born, he bestowed wealth upon them with due honor, saying:
"May this lord of the earth be as described; and when he reaches old age, may he depart for the forests."
Then, having understood through signs and by the power of his asceticism that birth had occurred for him who was to end the cycle of births,
the great seer Asita, thirsting for the True Dharma, came to the palace of the Lord of the Śākyas.

The king’s preceptor, with due respect and hospitality, ushered that knower of Brahman— who was himself a knower of Brahman and blazing with the splendor of the Veda as well as the splendor of asceticism— into the royal palace.
He, whose surge of joy had arisen at the birth of the prince, entered the vicinity of the king’s inner apartments;
yet, being steadfast, he did so as if by the designation of a forest, owing both to his excellence in asceticism and to the presence of old age.
Then the king, having properly honored that sage seated upon his throne with water for the feet and the arghya offering,
invited him according to the prescribed rites, just as Antideva once did for Vasiṣṭha.
"I am blessed; this family of mine is graced, since the Blessed One has come desiring to see me.
Let it be commanded, O gentle one, what shall I do? I am your disciple; you may place your full confidence in me."
Thus invited by the king with his whole being, the sage,
his wide eyes blossoming with wonder, spoke these words in a profound and steady manner, exactly as was appropriate.
This is worthy of you, a great soul, a lover of guests, generous, and desirous of dharma—
that my mind should be so affectionate toward me, in accordance with your character, lineage, wisdom, and age.
And this is how those royal sages,
having acquired wealth through subtle righteousness,
became rich in asceticism while remaining poor in material possessions, constantly renouncing it according to the prescribed rules.
Now hear from me the purpose for which I have come, and receive my words with joy:
"I have heard a divine voice in the path of the sun that a son has been born to you for the sake of awakening."
Having heard those words and having applied my mind, and then having understood through omens,
I have come here out of a desire to see the banner of the Śākya clan, which stands as high as the banner of Śakra.
Having heard these words, the lord of men, his gait agitated with great joy,
took the prince who was resting in the lap of his nurse and presented him to the one whose wealth is asceticism.

Then that great seer beheld the prince with wonder: his feet marked with wheels, his hands and feet with fingers and toes joined by webs, his eyebrows joined by a tuft of hair, and his male organ sheathed like that of an elephant.

Beholding him resting upon the nurse’s lap as if he were the son of Agni resting upon the lap of a goddess, his tears trembled at the edges of his eyelashes; and sighing, he turned his face toward the heavens.
Seeing Asita with eyes overflowing with tears,
the king trembled out of affection for his son;
with his body bowed and palms joined in reverence, he asked him with a faltering voice and a throat choked with sobs:

O steadfast one, why do you shed tears upon seeing him— his body but little different from that of the gods, his birth most wonderful and radiant, and of whom you have declared that his future purpose is supreme?
"O Blessed One, will the prince have a long life? Has he not been born for my sorrow?
Having somehow obtained this handful of water, will Time not surely come to drink it away? (Bc 1.64)
"Is this treasury of my fame indeed inexhaustible? Is this firm foundation of my family's prosperity secure?
Having slept with my son as my one unblinking eye, shall I go happily to the next world? (Buddhacarita 1.65)
I fear that this sprout of my family, though yet unfledged, may wither away before it has even blossomed.
O Lord, tell me quickly; I have no peace, for you surely know the affection that kinsmen feel for their child.
Perceiving that the king was overcome with agitation by the thought of what was undesirable, the sage spoke to him:
"O King, let there be no other thought in your mind; that which I have said is undoubtedly true."
I have no agitation regarding any change in him; rather, I am distressed because of my own deception.
For this time of mine has passed away, and he has been born as one who will understand the destruction of birth, which is so difficult to attain.
Having abandoned his kingdom and become indifferent toward sense-objects, he has realized the ultimate truth through intense efforts;
for he shall blaze as a sun composed of wisdom to destroy the darkness of delusion in the world.

He will rescue the distressed world, which is being swept away by the ocean of suffering— with its foam of scattered diseases, its waves of old age, and its fierce current of death— by means of the great raft of knowledge.

The world of living beings, tormented by thirst, shall drink from this supreme river of Dharma that has begun to flow— its current the force of wisdom, its embankment firm morality, its coolness meditative concentration, and its ruddy geese the vows.

For he will proclaim the path to liberation to those afflicted by suffering, obscured by sense objects, and situated on the wilderness paths of saṃsāra— just as one would to travelers who have lost their way.
To the people in this world who are being scorched by the fire of passion with sense objects as its fuel,
he will grant refreshment through the rain of Dharma, like a great cloud at the end of the summer heat with its downpour.

For the sake of the departure of living beings, he shall burst open with his supreme and unassailable mace of the True Dharma the door whose bolt is craving and whose panels are the darkness of delusion.
Having awakened for the sake of the world— which is enveloped by its own snares of delusion, overwhelmed by suffering, and without refuge— this King of Dharma will effect its liberation from bondage.

Therefore, do not feel grief on his account; rather, he is the one who should be mourned in this world of men—he who, out of delusion, attachment to sensual pleasures, or intoxication, shall not hear this ultimate Dharma.
Because I have fallen away from those virtues, even though I have attained the meditative absorptions, my purpose remains unfulfilled;
for I consider dwelling even in the triple heaven to be a misfortune, since I have not heard that Dharma.
Having heard this meaning, the king, together with his friends and his wife, abandoned his despondency and rejoiced;
for he thought, "Such is this son of mine," and thereby recognized his own excellence as well.
Thinking, "He will indeed proceed by the path of the Ṛṣis," he made his heart subject to anxiety;
for it was not that he did not favor the side of the beloved Dharma,
but rather that he perceived fear in the destruction of his lineage.
Then the sage Asita, having explained the truth concerning the son to the king who was so distressed for his child,
departed by way of the air just as he had come, his form watched with great respect and joy.
Having seen his son with his friends and having heard the words of the sage as well as his resolve,
that virtuous man, out of compassion, directed him in many ways like a beloved son.
The king also, delighted by the birth of his son, released the bonds affecting those within his realm;
and, as was fitting for his lineage, he duly performed the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) for his beloved son.
When ten days had passed, with a disciplined mind and filled with supreme joy,
he performed prayers, burnt offerings, auspicious rites, and sacrifices to the gods for the ultimate welfare of his son.

Moreover, for the sake of increasing his son's merit, he himself gave to the twice-born cows that were full in number— counting by the hundreds of thousands— possessing firm strength and vigor, adorned with golden horns, free from old age, and yielding abundant milk.
Then, having performed various rites that pleased his own heart,
the self-restrained prince, being joyful, set his mind upon entering the city at an auspicious, virtuous, and fixed moment.
Then, for the sake of her welfare, the queen, who possessed a son, bowed down to the deities and ascended a costly palanquin made of ivory, adorned with white and pale-pink flowers and jeweled lamps.
Having first ushered his wife— accompanied by elderly attendants and protected by her child— into the city,
the king also departed with the throngs of citizens, being honored like Maghavan by the immortals ascending to heaven.

Then, having entered the palace, the King of the Śākyas—resembling Śiva rejoicing at the birth of the six-faced Kārttikeya—with a face full of joy, performed various acts that brought prosperity and renown, exclaiming, "This! This! Bc_1.88.
Thus, through the birth and prosperity of the king’s son, that city named Kapila, together with its countryside,
became as joyful as the city of Kubera when Nalakūbara was born, being strewn with celestial nymphs.
Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Birth of the Blessed One," in the great epic poem *Buddhacarita*.
From the birth of that son— who had conquered his own self and brought an end to birth and old age—
that king increased day by day in wealth, elephants, horses, and allies, like the ocean by the force of its waters.
Then indeed he obtained many treasures of wealth and various jewels, as well as wrought and unwrought gold— treasures that were too great a burden even for his desires.

Even those lords of elephants from the Himalayas, intoxicated with rut and resembling lotuses, who were unable to enter this circle even with great effort, approached him spontaneously without any exertion.
His city was agitated by horses adorned with various marks and emblems, with ornaments of fresh gold, with long manes, and others acquired through military force, friendship, and wealth.
In his kingdom, there were many cows— well-nourished, contented, virtuous, free from dust,
and yielding milk of excellent quality— who were accompanied by vigorous calves and yielded much milk.
His enemy became neutral; the neutral one turned into a friend;
his ally attained a state of particular firmness; and as for the other two sides, they ceased to exist.

Likewise, at the proper time and in the proper place, the god sent down rain with gentle breezes and the sound of clouds, the sky adorned by lightning for its earrings, and free from the evils of falling stones, showers of dust, or thunderbolts.
The crops grew fruitful according to the season through his labor in agriculture alone;
moreover, those very medicinal herbs became superior in both sap and essence.
Even at a time that threatened their very lives, as if a tumultuous battle had broken out,
women gave birth easily, healthily, and without affliction, by the power of time.
Even when their own wealth was contemptible, men did not beg from others who observed separate vows;
and at that time, no noble person turned away, even when requested for a mere trifle.
In his kingdom, there was no one who lacked respect for kinsmen, nor anyone who was stingy, nor one who failed to observe vows, nor a liar, nor a violent person—
just as it was in the realm of King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa.
And there, desiring the Dharma and having directly perceived the existence of heaven, they performed acts of merit for gardens, temples, hermitages, wells, water-stations, lotus ponds, and groves.
Freed from the fears of famine and disease, the joyful people rejoiced as if in heaven;
and neither husband nor wife, nor queen nor lord, ever strayed from one another.

Some pursued pleasure but not for the sake of desire; some guarded wealth but not for the sake of desire; some practiced dharma but not for the sake of wealth; and some committed violence but not for the sake of dharma.
His own realm was freed from thieves and enemies, became healthy and liberated from foreign armies;
it became secure and well-supplied with food, just like the kingdom of Purāṇaraṇya.
For at that time, in the birth of that king, as in the kingdom of Manu, the son of Aditya,
joy prevailed, evil perished, dharma blazed forth, and impurity was stilled.
Since such prosperity of the royal family and the accomplishment of all aims had arisen from him,
the king therefore gave his son the name Sarvārthasiddha.
But Queen Māyā, beholding her son’s vast power which was like that of the foremost of the gods, was unable to endure the joy that had arisen; she then departed for heaven to dwell there.

Then his maternal aunt, whose power was equal to that of his mother, raised the prince— who was like the offspring of a god— with affection and devotion no different from her own, as if he were her own son.
Then that prince grew up properly and gradually, like the young sun rising on the horizon, like fire fanned by the wind, or like the lord of the stars in a cloudless fortnight.
Then, from the homes of their friends, they brought for him highly precious sandalwood, strings of jewels filled with medicinal herbs, and golden chariots yoked with deer.
He gave ornaments suited to their ages, golden elephants, deer, and horses,
chariots yoked with toy oxen, and dolls variegated with gold and silver.
Thus, being attended to by those various services appropriate to his age,
though he was but a child, he became like one who was not a child in steadfastness, purity, intellect, and splendor.

Having properly passed beyond childhood and having reached at the right time the duty of practical application, he acquired in a few days the sciences appropriate to his lineage, which would normally take many years to master.
Having heard from the great seer Asita that his son’s future welfare would be supreme,
the Śākya king conceived an attachment to sensual pleasures, thinking, "May he go to the forests."

Then, from a family endowed with steadfast virtue, he summoned for him a noble woman named Yaśodharā— vast in fame, possessed of beauty, modesty, and humility— who was like the goddess Śrī herself under the name Vāmā.
Shining with a supreme form, the prince, who resembled Sanatkumāra,
took his delight together with that bride of the Śākya king, as the thousand-eyed Indra does with Śacī.
Reflecting on how he might not encounter anything adverse that could disturb his mind,
the king assigned him a residence within the inner apartments of the palace, rather than allowing him to roam upon the earth.
Then, in palaces as white as autumn clouds, colored like celestial chariots upon the earth—
mansions providing comfort in all seasons— he sported with noble musical instruments accompanied by women.
With mṛdaṅga drums bound with golden girdles and struck by the fingertips of women,
and with dances equal to the performances of the finest apsarases, that palace shone like Kailāsa.

There, the women delighted him with their words, artistic gestures, playful dalliances, amorous coquetties, intoxication, sportive movements, and sweet laughter; they did so also with deceptive charms and sidelong glances.
Then, seized by women skilled in the arts of love and fierce in their passion,
he did not descend from the back of the celestial chariot to the earth, just as one of meritorious deeds does not descend from the back of a celestial chariot.
But the king, impelled by the very cause of the prince’s growth and by the destiny that was to come to pass,
took delight in tranquility, desisted from evil, practiced self-restraint, and honored the virtuous.
He did not cling to the pleasures of the senses like one who is fickle, nor did he feel excessive passion for his mother;
with fortitude he conquered the restless horses of the senses, and he won over his kinsmen and citizens through his virtues.
He did not study knowledge for the suffering of another; rather, he studied that auspicious wisdom which is beneficial.
For just as he wished for the welfare of his own subjects, so too did he desire the auspicious for all beings.
Then, for the sake of long life, he duly worshipped the radiant Bhaṃ, the presiding deity of Aṅgiras;
he offered oblations into the unextinguished fire and bestowed pearls and cows upon the twice-born.
He bathed his body to purify both mind and person with the waters of sacred fords and the waters of virtue;
and he drank the Soma prescribed by the Vedas, as well as his own son, who was like unto himself, and the peace and bliss of his heart.
He spoke with gentleness, yet it was not devoid of meaning; he uttered what was true, yet not unpleasant.
For out of shame, he was unable to speak even to himself words that were gentle but untrue, or harsh though they were the truth.
Regarding matters that were desirable or undesirable, he did not fall under the sway of passion or aversion;
he practiced auspicious conduct purified by worldly propriety, for he valued such ritual action more highly than the sacrifice itself.
To one who approached him with hope, he immediately severed thirst with the waters he gave;
and apart from battle, he shattered the arrogant pride of his enemies with the axe of his conduct.
He disciplined one [of the two], he protected seven, he abandoned seven, and he guarded five;
he attained the threefold set, he understood the threefold set, he realized the twofold set, and he cast off the twofold set.
Even when they had committed offenses and were condemned to death, he did not have them executed, nor did he look upon them with anger;
instead, he bound them with kind words and rewards, for even their release was seen by him as leading to their ruin.
He practiced the supreme vows of the seers and cast off long-accumulated enmities;
he acquired glories fragrant with virtue and shed the dust that causes defilement.
He did not desire to seize Bali when he was not offering himself; he did not intend to covet the property of others;
he did not wish to speak of the unrighteousness of his enemies; nor did he harbor anger in his heart.
When the lord of the earth had thus set out, his servants and citizens likewise conducted themselves in that same manner,
just as the senses of one engaged in yoga behave when the mind is tranquil and serene.
Then, in due time, to Yaśodharā— who possessed beautiful breasts and was the upholder of her own fame—
the son of Śuddhodana begot a son who had a face like that of the enemy of Rāhu (the sun), and who was named Rāhula.
Then the protector of the earth, whose desire for a son had been fulfilled, was supremely delighted regarding the prosperity of his lineage;
he rejoiced at the birth of a grandson just as he had rejoiced at the birth of a son.
Thinking, "How might my affection for my son become as focused on him as it is on myself? he was filled with joy;
and in due time, that lover of his son undertook various rites, like one desiring to ascend to heaven.
Abiding on the path of the illustrious preeminent kings of the first eon,
he performed austerities without uttering even a single word, and he sacrificed with rituals free from violence.
Then that man of meritorious deeds blazed forth with both royal splendor and the splendor of asceticism;
radiant in lineage, conduct, and intellect, he was like the thousand-rayed sun about to release its brilliance.
Having worshipped the *Arcika* hymn of Svayambhū, he who was established in prosperity chanted it for the sake of his son’s stability;
and desiring to create offspring, he performed difficult rites, like a creator in the primordial age.
He laid aside the sword and pondered the scriptures; he cultivated tranquility and endured self-restraint.
Like one who has mastered his senses, he did not pursue any object of desire; like a father, he looked upon all objects with equanimity.
For he bore the kingdom for the sake of a son; a son for the sake of the lineage; the lineage for the sake of fame;
fame for the sake of heaven; heaven for the sake of the self; and he desired the maintenance of the self for the sake of dharma.
Thus he employed various means, established by tradition and proven by scripture, hoping and entreating:
"How might my son, having seen his father's face, not go to the forest? (Bc 2.54)
On this earth, kings who desire to preserve the royal fortune established within themselves protect their sons;
yet that lord of men, desiring righteousness, protected his son from unrighteousness by releasing him from sensual objects.
All those Bodhisattvas of incomparable being, having experienced the flavor of sensual pleasure and having fathered sons, departed for the forest;
therefore, although the cause was firmly rooted, he who had accumulated such karma continued to indulge in delight until he attained awakening.
Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Residence in the Inner Apartments," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.
Then, on one occasion, he heard of forests adorned with lotus-pools, where the trees resounded with the calls of male cuckoos and the grass was soft and lush, all set to the accompaniment of songs.
Then, having heard of the charming qualities of the city groves that are so dear to women,
he set his mind on going outside, like an elephant confined within its stall.
Then the king, having understood the disposition of that desire called "son," ordered an excursion to the pleasure gardens, which was appropriate for his affection, his prosperity, and his age.
And he caused the throng of distressed commoners on the royal road to turn back,
thinking, "Lest the prince, whose mind is so delicate, become agitated in heart."
Then, with the utmost gentleness, they removed from all directions those who were deficient in limbs, those with impaired faculties, the aged, the sick, and the wretched,
thereby bringing about the supreme splendor of the royal road.
Then, when the magnificent royal road had been prepared, the illustrious prince, accompanied by humble attendants,
descended from the roof of the palace at the proper time and, having received permission, approached the king.

Then the lord of men, with tears welling up, smelled his son's head, gazed at him for a long time, and commanded him with his voice, "Go"; yet out of affection, he did not release him even in his mind.
Then he ascended a golden chariot yoked with four quiet horses that bore vessels of Jāmbūnada gold, which possessed the pure radiance of a hero, a scholar, and a saint.

Then, accompanied by a fitting retinue, he set out upon a path strewn with clusters of radiant flowers, adorned with suspended garlands, and graced with fluttering banners— just as the moon, together with the stars, enters the firmament.
He slowly entered the royal road while being gazed upon from all sides by the citizens with eyes wide with curiosity, as if they were scattering half-open blue lotuses.

Some praised him for his gentle qualities, while others worshipped him for his brilliance; some, because of his gracious countenance, extolled his splendor, and others wished him long life in its full abundance.
Hunchbacked women emerged from noble families, and troops of Kirātas and dwarfs;
women also came forth from humble dwellings and bowed down like the banners in the procession of the gods.
Then, having heard from the servants the news that the prince was indeed departing, the women,
permitted by their respectable elders, went to the roofs of the palaces out of a desire to see him.
Hindered by their slipping girdle-strings, with eyes agitated as if waking from sleep,
and having rearranged their ornaments according to the circumstances, they surrounded him restlessly out of curiosity.

Frightening the flocks of domestic birds with the echoes from the stairs and floors of the palaces, the tinkling of their girdles, and the clatter of their anklets, they jostled one another with great speed.
But among some of these excellent women, though they were filled with haste and eager anticipation,
their broad hips and full breasts checked their progress due to their own weight.
Although she was capable of moving quickly, she restrained herself and did not go fast;
bashful and unaccustomed to it, she concealed the ornaments she had put on for the private occasion.
Then, as those women pressed against one another and crowded together, their earrings agitated by the friction and their ornaments jingling, there was no peace at the windows.
The lotus-faces of the women, with their earrings brushing against one another as they leaned out from the windows, shone like lotuses clinging to the palace rooftops.
Then, with palanquins borne by young women and their windows opened out of curiosity,
the glorious city shone on all sides like the sky filled with celestial chariots accompanied by Apsarases.
Because the windows were not wide, the faces of those filled with supreme joy, their earrings resting against one another’s cheeks, shone like clusters of lotuses tied together.
Beholding the prince on the road, those women appeared as if they wished to go to the earth;
and the men, looking up at him with faces turned upward, appeared as if they wished to go to heaven.
And having seen that prince, blazing with his physical form and splendor, those women softly said,
"Blessed is his wife," with pure minds indeed and not from any other motive.
"This man, indeed, with his long and muscular arms, is like the God of Love himself in beauty;
having abandoned worldly splendor, he will attain the Dharma"—thinking thus, they showed him nothing but reverence.
Having first beheld the royal highway strewn with humble citizens of pure and resolute appearance, the prince rejoiced slightly and thought as if he were to experience a new birth for himself.
But seeing that city as joyful as heaven, the gods dwelling in the Pure Abodes fashioned an old man in order to incite the son of the king to depart.
Then the prince, seeing him overcome by old age and his form distinct from that of other men,
spoke to his charioteer while remaining there with his gaze fixed unwaveringly upon him.

"O charioteer, who is this man who has approached us, with white hair, holding a staff for support, his eyes hidden by his brows, his limbs slack and bent? Is this a transformation, his natural state, or a mere accident? (Buddhacarita 3.28)
Thus addressed, the charioteer, perceiving no fault even in that which ought to have been concealed, reported the matter to the prince; his own discernment having been clouded by those very gods.
The destroyer of beauty, the ruin of strength, the source of sorrow, the end of pleasures,
the destruction of memories, and the enemy of the senses— this is what is called old age, by which he has been broken.
For even by him milk was drunk in childhood; in the course of time he crawled further upon the earth;
having gradually become a handsome youth, he has in that very same sequence reached old age.
When this had been said, the prince moved slightly and spoke thus to the charioteer:
"Will this same affliction befall me as well? Thereupon, the charioteer replied to him:
"Even for the Venerable One, this advanced age will undoubtedly come about through the power of time;
thus the world both knows and accepts that old age is the destroyer of beauty. (Bc 3.33)
Then that Great-Souled One, whose intellect was purified by past aspirations and who had accumulated meritorious deeds throughout vast eons,
trembled upon hearing of old age, like a cow at the sound of a great thunderclap nearby.

Sighing deeply and shaking his head, fixing his gaze upon that old man and seeing the joyful multitude, he spoke these words with agitation: niḥśvasya dīrghaṃ svaśiraḥ prakampya tasmiṃśca jīrṇe viniveśya cakṣuḥ / tāṃ caiva dṛṣṭvā janatāṃ saharṣāṃ vākyaṃ sa saṃvigna idaṃ jagāda // Bc_3.35 //
Thus old age destroys memory, beauty, and prowess without distinction;
yet the world does not experience a sense of spiritual urgency, even while witnessing such things directly before its eyes.
"Since this is so, charioteer, turn back the horses; you must proceed quickly to our home.
For how could there be delight for me in the grounds of a pleasure garden when the fear of old age dwells within my mind? (Buddhacarita 3.37)
Then, at the command of his father’s son, the charioteer turned the chariot back;
thereupon the prince returned to that very palace, which, under the sway of anxiety, seemed to him as if empty.
But when he found no peace even there, examining [the world] again and again with the thought "old age, old age," he then,
with the permission of the king, went out once more by that same path in due course.
Then those same gods created another man whose body was overwhelmed by disease;
and seeing him, the son of Śuddhodana, his gaze fixed intently upon him, spoke to the charioteer.
"With a large belly, a body trembling from labored breathing, shoulders and arms drooping, and limbs thin and pale—
who is this man, uttering the piteous word 'Mother' while leaning upon another?"

Then the charioteer said to him: "O gentle one, this is a great calamity called 'disease,' which has arisen from the aggravation of the bodily humors and has increased until it has rendered even this man, though otherwise capable, no longer independent."
Having spoken thus, the prince, looking again at that man with compassion, said:
"This fault has arisen in him alone; the fear of disease is common to all living beings."
Then the charioteer said: "O Prince, this affliction is common to all;
for even when tormented by diseases, the world, overcome by pain, still seeks after joy."
Having heard this meaning, his heart despondent, he trembled like the moon reflected in the waves of the ocean;
and feeling compassion, he spoke these words in a somewhat gentle voice: Bc_3.45 //

Beholding this calamity of disease among living beings, people nevertheless place their trust [in life]; alas, how vast is the ignorance of men! Those who are not yet freed from the fears of disease laugh [at others].
"Charioteer, let us turn back from this journey outside; let the chariot proceed only to the king's palace.
Having heard of the fear of disease, my heart, repelled from pleasures, seems to shrink away."
Then, having turned back with his joy departed, he entered his palace lost in deep reflection.
Seeing him thus returned, the lord of the earth conducted a search for him.
Having heard the omen of his return, he considered himself already abandoned by him;
and though enraged, he did not inflict severe punishment upon the official in charge of the road's cleanliness.
Furthermore, fearing that he might become attached due to his restless senses and thus abandon us, the king provided his son with even greater indulgence in sensual pleasures.
And when his son found no delight at all within the inner apartments due to the objects of the senses, such as sounds and the rest,
he then ordered an excursion outside, thinking that there might be a different kind of aesthetic experience.
And perceiving his son’s disposition through affection, and disregarding certain faults of passion,
he commanded those courtesans who were skilled in the arts and proficient therein.
Then, on the royal highway, which was specially decorated and inspected,
the king, having caused the charioteer and the chariot to be turned back, sent the prince outside.
Then, as the prince was proceeding in that manner, those very gods caused a corpse to appear;
on that very road, the charioteer and the prince saw the dead man being carried along, and no one else did.
Then the prince said to the charioteer: "Who is this man being carried by four men, followed by dejected people, who, though adorned, is weeping?"
Then the Charioteer, his mind overcome by those gods of pure nature and pure abodes,
spoke this matter— which was otherwise unspeakable— to the Lord in meaningful words.
Deprived of the faculties of intellect, senses, and vital breaths, asleep and unconscious, become like grass or wood—
this certain being, though nurtured and protected with great effort by those dear to him, is now abandoned.
Having heard these words of the guide, he was somewhat agitated and said to him:
"Is this dharma for this person alone, or is such an end common to all living beings?"
Then the charioteer said to him: "This is the end of all living beings;
whether lowly, middling, or great-souled, for everyone in the world, destruction is certain."
Then that prince, though steadfast, immediately despaired upon hearing of his own death;
leaning his shoulder against the tip of the chariot pole, he spoke in a resonant voice: Bc_3.60.
This is the certain end for all living beings, yet the world remains heedless and casts off fear;
I suspect the hearts of men are hard, for they proceed along this path as if they were secure.
Therefore, charioteer, let our chariot be turned back from the pleasure grounds; for this is neither the right place nor the right time.
Knowing of our impending destruction, how could one who possesses consciousness remain heedless here at a time of distress?
Even though the son of the lord of men spoke thus, he did not turn that chariot back;
however, by the command of the king, he drove forth toward the forest itself, specifically toward the grove of lotus-beds.

Then he beheld that forest, which was like the Nandana grove, auspicious with its flowering young trees, filled with wandering, joyful, and intoxicated cuckoos, and possessing lotus-filled ponds as beautiful as celestial chariots.
Then the prince was forcibly led into that forest thick with throngs of beautiful women,
like a newly initiated ascetic, fearful of obstacles, being led by force to the abode of the Lord of Alakā, which is surrounded by excellent apsarases.
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Arising of Worldly Disenchantment," in the great epic poem *Buddhacarita*.
Then, from that city garden, women with eyes flickering with curiosity went out to meet the prince as he arrived, like brides meeting their bridegroom.
Having approached him, their eyes wide with wonder,
they performed the customary rites of hospitality with hands resembling the buds of lotuses.
And they stood surrounding him, their hearts captivated by love,
as if drinking him in with eyes that were motionless yet blossoming with affection.
For the women thought of him as Desire personified,
adorned with radiant innate marks as if with ornaments.
And because of his gentleness and fortitude,
some recognized him as the moon itself descended to earth with its rays concealed.
Overwhelmed by his physical beauty, those women yawned as if their spirits were subdued;
striking one another with their glances, they sighed softly.
Thus those women merely beheld him with their sight;
they neither spoke nor laughed, being restrained by his majestic power.
Seeing them thus inactive and overwhelmed by affection,
the wise son of the family priest, Udāyin, spoke these words:
"You all possess knowledge of every art, are experts in perceiving the inner state of beings,
are endowed with beauty and skill, and have attained preeminence through your own virtues."
By these virtues, he would have outshone even the inhabitants of Uttarakuru,
as well as the pleasure garden of Kubera, let alone this very earth.
You are capable of moving even sages who are free from passion,
and you are able to capture even the gods when they are accompanied by celestial nymphs.
By means of your knowledge of dispositions, your gestures, and your perfection of physical charm,
you are capable of inflaming passion even in women— how much more so, then, in men?
"Such is the behavior of you who, being separated from your own proper sphere, act in this manner; I am not pleased with your honesty."
This conduct of yours, with eyes downcast in modesty, would indeed be fitting for newlywed brides, or perhaps for the wives of cowherds.
Even if this wise man were great due to the power of his splendor,
one must reach the certain conclusion that even for women, there is great majesty here.
For in the past, the great seer Vyāsa, who was unassailable even by the gods, was kicked with his foot by Kāśisundarī, a courtesan.
In former times, the monk Manthālagautama, desiring to please a courtesan with his own leg, sacrificed his life for her sake.
A woman, though inferior in both caste and station, gratified the great seer Gautama, who was long-lived and practiced long austerities.
In the same way, Śāntā captivated and carried off Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, the son of a sage, who was likewise unskilled with women, by means of various stratagems.
And the great seer Viśvāmitra, though he had plunged into profound austerity,
was carried away for ten years by the Apsaras Ghṛtācī through his passion.
In this way, women brought even those various sages to a state of transformation;
how much more so, then, the king’s son, who was youthful and full of charm?
This being so, you must therefore strive with confidence in such a way that this glory of the king’s lineage does not turn its back on us.
For those young women who captivate a person of their own kind are merely women;
but those who seize the hearts of both the lowly and the exalted are truly [divine] women.
Having heard these words of Udāyin, those women, as if pierced by arrows,
resolved their minds upon seizing the prince.
With their glances, gestures, smiles, coquettish movements,
and gait, those women performed provocative actions as if they were trembling with fear.
But due to the king’s command and the prince’s gentleness,
as well as through intoxication and passion, they quickly abandoned their lack of trust.
Then the prince, surrounded by a company of women, roamed the forest like an elephant accompanied by a herd of females in the Himalayan woods.
Preceded by his women, he blazed forth in that delightful grove like the radiant sun surrounded by apsarases in the Ākrīḍa garden.
There, some women, overcome by passion,
touched him with their firm, full, compact, and lovely breasts.
A certain woman, her soft vine-like arms hanging down languidly from her drooping shoulders,
forcibly embraced him after he had uttered a faltering falsehood.
One woman, with her copper-red lower lip and mouth fragrant with wine, whispered into his ear: "Listen to a secret."
One woman, her body anointed with unguents, spoke as if giving a command:
"Devote yourself here," desiring to take hold of his hand.
Another woman, whose blue garment had repeatedly slipped away under the pretext of intoxication,
shone with her girdle visible, like a night streaked with flashing lightning.
Some wandered here and there, their golden girdles jingling,
displaying to him their hips covered with thin garments.
Others, grasping flowering mango branches, leaned forward,
displaying their breasts which resembled golden jars.
A certain lotus-eyed woman, having come from a lotus grove with a lotus in her hand,
stood by his side as he sat there like the goddess Padmaśrī beside the lotus-faced one.
A certain woman sang a sweet song, full of meaning and accompanied by gestures,
as if urging him— who was so composed— to wake up with her glances, saying, "You have been deceived."
Another woman, with her beautiful face drawing back the bow of her eyebrows,
imitated his gesture with a steady and playful grace.
A certain woman with full, lovely breasts and earrings swaying as she laughed,
laughed loudly at him, saying, "May you find fulfillment!"
Likewise, others bound him as he was departing with garlands of flowers;
some seized him with the goads of sweet words mixed with reproach.
Seeking a rival, a certain woman, holding a mango branch and overcome by intoxication, asked: "To whom does this flower belong?"
One woman, assuming a masculine gait and even a masculine posture, said to him: "Men have been conquered by women; now, O sir, conquer this earth!"
Then a certain woman with tremulous eyes, smelling a blue lotus,
addressed the prince with words slightly faltering from intoxication:
Behold, my lord, the mango tree covered with flowers fragrant as honey,
where the cuckoo sings like one confined within a golden cage.
"Behold this Ashoka tree, which increases the sorrow of those who desire;
here the bees cry out as if they were being consumed by fire. (Bc 4.45)
Behold the *tilaka* tree embraced by a mango branch,
like a man dressed in white garments embraced by a woman with yellow unguents on her limbs.
Behold the blossoming *kurubaka* flower, with a luster like used lac;
it seems to bow down as if to mock the radiance of women’s nails.
And behold this young *aśoka* tree, covered with new shoots,
which stands as if ashamed by the beauty of our hands.
Behold the long pond covered by *sinduvāra* trees growing on its banks,
like a young woman lying down, draped in white silken garments.
Behold the greatness found even among women: for here is this cakravāka bird following his mate in the water, trailing behind her like a servant.
"Listen to the sound of this intoxicated cuckoo as it cries;
another cuckoo immediately calls back to it, as if in an echo. (Bc 4.51)
Indeed, the intoxication of birds is brought on by spring;
but it is not so for a person who considers himself wise yet ponders upon the inconceivable.
Thus, those young women, their minds unrestrained by the god of love,
assailed the prince with various such stratagems.
Though thus provoked, he whose senses were shrouded by fortitude felt neither joy nor pain; though agitated by the thought that he must die, he neither rejoiced nor was distressed.
Seeing their lack of stability in reality, that Supreme Person reflected with a mind that was both composed and agitated.
But these women do not realize that youth is fickle, for they are intoxicated by their own beauty, which old age will surely destroy.
Surely these people do not perceive the onset of disease in anyone; thus they are joyful, having cast aside fear in a world whose very nature is afflicted by illness.
And clearly unaware of death, which carries away everything, they remain at ease and free from anxiety, playing and laughing. (Bc 4.58)
For what conscious person, knowing of old age, disease, and death,
would remain at ease, sit down, or lie down— much less laugh?
But he who, having seen another who is aged, diseased, or even dead,
remains healthy and undisturbed, is exactly like one who is devoid of consciousness.
For when a tree is being separated from its flowers or even its fruits,
or when it falls or is cut down, another tree does not grieve.
Seeing him thus devoted to meditation and devoid of longing for sense objects,
Udāyin, who was learned in the treatises on ethics, spoke to him out of friendship:
"I have indeed been granted by the king as a worthy friend to you; therefore, because of that affectionate regard, I desire to speak with you. (Bc 4.63)
Preventing one from what is harmful, encouraging engagement in what is beneficial,
and not abandoning one in times of misfortune— this is the threefold characteristic of a friend.
Having thus pledged my love, if I were to turn away from human effort and neglect you,
there would be no true friendship in me.
Therefore, acting as a friend, I say this to you, who are young and handsome:
such lack of courtesy toward women is not befitting of you.
It is even proper for men to comply with women through falsehood,
both for the sake of avoiding their shame and for the sake of one's own pleasure.
Humility and compliance are the means by which women bind the heart;
for these are the sources of affection, yet women desire honor.
Therefore, O large-eyed one, even though your heart is turned away,
you ought to comply with courtesy that is befitting of this beauty.
Courtesy is the medicine for women; courtesy is their supreme ornament.
Beauty devoid of courtesy is like a forest without flowers.
Or rather, let there be acceptance out of mere courtesy or affection;
for having obtained objects so difficult to find, you ought not to treat them with contempt.
Knowing that sensual pleasure is supreme, even the god Purandara once lusted after Ahalyā,
the wife of the sage Gautama.
Agastya sought Rohiṇī, the wife of Soma;
therefore, according to sacred tradition, he obtained Lopāmudrā, who was her equal.
And this man of great asceticism, my maternal grandfather,
Bharadvāja, was begotten by Bṛhaspati upon Mārutī, the wife of Utathya.
And while Bṛhaspati’s queen was offering oblations,
the Moon, the best of sacrificers, begat Budha, whose deeds were those of a wise deity.
And long ago, on the bank of the Yamunā, Parāśara, having conceived a passion, approached the maiden Kālī, who was born from the waters.
Out of a desire for dalliance with the censured Mātaṅgī, the Apsaras Akṣamālā,
the sage Vasiṣṭha begot a son named Kapiñjalāda.
And even when his youth had passed away, the royal sage Yayāti took delight with the Apsaras Viśvācī in the Caitraratha forest.
Although the Kuru prince Pāṇḍu knew that association with women ends in destruction,
he was captivated by the beauty and virtues of Mādrī and indulged in the pleasure born of desire.
And Karālajanaka likewise, having abducted a Brahmin’s daughter, suffered such a downfall; yet he did not cease to pursue the god of love. (Bc 4.80)
In this way, these great-souled ones enjoyed even objects of sense that were censurable for the sake of pleasure, let alone those endowed with excellent qualities.
Yet you, though powerful, handsome, and young, rightly reject the sense-objects which this world is so deeply attached to. (Bc 4.82)
Having heard these words of his, which were gentle and consistent with the scriptures,
the prince, whose voice was like the roar of thunder, replied:
These words of yours are appropriate and reveal your affection;
and I shall persuade you regarding that matter concerning which you think poorly of me.
I do not despise sense objects, for I know the world to be composed of them;
yet, having perceived the world as impermanent, my mind finds no delight therein.
If these three— old age, disease, and death— did not exist,
then even for me there would be delight in charming sense-objects.
Even if this very body of women were eternal,
my mind might well take pleasure in sensual desires, despite their being full of faults.
But when their beauty has been swallowed up by old age, it will become even to themselves something undesirable; yet, out of delusion, they find pleasure therein.
Subject to death, disease, and old age, yet taking pleasure with those whose very nature is death, disease, and old age, he remained undisturbed and equal to the beasts and birds.
As for what you said— that even those great souls were possessed by desire— one should feel a sense of spiritual urgency precisely regarding this, since even they experienced their destruction.
I do not consider that to be greatness where there is general decline, or attachment to sense objects, or a lack of composure through self-mastery. (Bc 4.91)
As for what you said— that one should deal with women even by means of falsehood—
I do not understand any such falsehood, even when it comes to courtesy.
Nor is compliance pleasing to me where there is no uprightness;
if there is no association with the whole being [of another], then shame on that!
For one who lacks steadfastness, who possesses faith yet is attached and sees no fault—what indeed could there be to deceive a mind in which passion has already arisen? (Bc 4.94)
If those who have conceived passion thus deceive one another,
then it is surely not fit for men to look at women, nor for women to look at men.
This being so, you ought not to entice me— afflicted by suffering and subject to old age and death— toward ignoble sensual pleasures.
"Aha! Your mind is exceedingly steadfast and powerful, for you perceive the essence even in fleeting desires.
Yet, while observing all beings on the path of death, you remain attached to sense objects that bring such intense fear."

But I, being timid and exceedingly distressed, reflecting upon the fear of old age, calamity, and disease, find neither peace nor fortitude; how could I find delight, beholding the world as if it were ablaze with fire?

I consider the consciousness of that man to be made of iron, who—knowing for certain that death is inevitable—yet conceives passion in his heart; he who does not weep but rejoices in the face of such great terror.
Then the prince delivered a discourse characterized by certainty, which destroys reliance upon sensual desires;
meanwhile, the sun, whose orb was pleasing to the eyes of the people, went down to the mountain of setting.
Then, their ornaments and garlands worn in vain, their artistic skills and amorous advances rendered fruitless,
the women returned to the city with their hopes shattered, having restrained the god of love within their own hearts.
Then, having observed the splendor of the people gathered in the city gardens, which was withdrawn again at evening,
the son of the protector of the earth entered his palace, reflecting upon the universality of impermanence.
Then, having heard that his mind was averse to the objects of the senses, the king could not sleep that night, like an elephant with a dart lodged in its heart.
Then, exhausted by the deliberations involving many diverse paths, he remained with his ministers.
He saw no other restraint for his son, whose mind was set on liberation, than [the renunciation of] sensual pleasures.
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Warding Off of the Women," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.

Though thus enticed by objects of the highest excellence, that son of the Śākya king found no steadfastness nor did he obtain peace; he was like a lion pierced in the heart by a deeply poisoned arrow.
Then, once followed by his sons, who were ministers’ sons— men of patience and varied conversation—
he set out from the city with the king’s permission, desiring to see the forest lands and longing for tranquility.

Having mounted the noble horse Kaṇṭhaka, who was adorned with a bridle of new gold and small bells, and whose beautiful golden trappings jingled as they moved, he set forth like the moon, the banner of the lotus-tree, ascending its own standard.
Drawn by his longing for the forest and by the virtues of the earth, he went further into the depths of the woodland;
there he beheld the ground being ploughed, its furrows like the shifting ripples upon the surface of water.

Beholding the earth in such a state— its grass and darbha blades torn up and scattered, and strewn with tiny insects, worms, and creatures that had been killed— he grieved intensely as if for the slaughter of his own kin.

Beholding the men plowing, their complexions discolored by the dust stirred up by the wind and the sun’s rays, and seeing the draft animals distressed by the exhaustion of pulling the load, the Supreme Noble One felt the highest compassion.
Then, descending from the back of his horse, he wandered slowly through the villages, overcome with grief;
reflecting upon the birth and passing away of the world, he spoke in distress, "Alas, this is truly miserable!"
Desiring mental solitude, he turned back those friends who followed him and went to the foot of a rose-apple tree in a secluded spot, which was covered on all sides with swaying, beautiful leaves.
He sat down upon a pure ground covered with grass as bright as lapis lazuli;
there, while investigating the origin and passing away of the world, he took hold of the path of mental stability.
Having immediately attained stability of mind and being liberated from afflictions such as the desire for sense objects,
he reached the first dhyāna— tranquil, accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and of an untainted nature.
Then, having attained the supreme joy and bliss born of seclusion— the concentration of mind—
he thereafter applied his thoughts even further to this very matter, having correctly observed the course of the world with his mind.
Alas, how pitiable it is that a person, being himself powerless and subject to the laws of disease, old age, and destruction,
yet blinded by intoxication and ignorant of the truth, feels revulsion toward another who is afflicted by old age, diseased, or dead.
If, being myself such as I am, I were to feel loathing for another who possesses such a nature,
it would be neither fitting nor appropriate for me who understands this supreme Dharma.
Thus, as he correctly perceived the defects of disease, old age, and misfortune pervading the world,
the pride residing within him regarding his own strength, youth, and life vanished in an instant.
He did not rejoice, nor did he feel remorse; he fell neither into doubt nor into sloth and sleep.
He was not attached to the qualities of sensual desire, nor did he harbor hatred, nor did he despise others.
Thus this stainless and pure understanding grew within that Great-Souled One;
and a man dressed as a mendicant, unseen by other men, approached him.
The son of the lord of men asked him, "Tell me, who are you? He then replied to him:
"O bull among men, terrified by birth and death, I am a wandering mendicant who has gone forth for the sake of liberation."
In this world subject to decay, I, seeking liberation, search for that auspicious and imperishable state;
with an equal mind toward my own kin and strangers, I have turned away from sense objects, with passion and hatred stilled.
Dwelling anywhere— at the foot of a tree, in a deserted shrine, on a mountain, or in a forest—
I wander about without possessions and free from expectations, seeking the ultimate truth and subsisting on whatever alms are obtained.
Having spoken this to the prince while he was still watching, he flew up into the sky;
for that celestial being, who had previously seen another Buddha in that very form, had come there for the sake of his remembrance.
As he moved through the sky like a bird, that best of men rejoiced and was filled with wonder;
then, having gained a clear understanding of the concept of Dharma, he set his mind upon the method for final liberation.
Then he, equal to Indra and having conquered the horses of his senses, mounted his horse intending to enter the city;
yet, looking back at his retinue, he did not proceed to the desired forest from that very spot.

Desiring to bring about the end of old age and death, he fixed his mind upon dwelling in the forest; he entered the city again not out of desire, but like a lordly elephant returning from the forest to the enclosure.
"O long-eyed one, happy indeed and blessed is that woman whose husband here is such as you!"—
thus the princess spoke with joined palms as she gazed at him while he was entering on the road.
Then he whose voice was like the roar of a great cloud heard this cry and attained supreme tranquility;
for having heard the word "nirvṛta," he set his mind upon the manner of final nirvāṇa.
Then he, whose body was like the peak of a mountain of gold, whose arms, voice, and eyes were like those of an elephant, a cloud,
and a bull respectively, and who possessed the countenance and prowess of the moon and a lion, attained his end while his passion for the imperishable Dharma had been born.
Then, with the gait of a king of beasts, he approached the monarch who was being attended by his circle of ministers,
like Sanatkumāra approaching Indra blazing in the assembly of the Maruts in the third heaven.
Having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, he spoke: "O god among men, grant me your gracious permission;
I wish to go forth into the religious life for the sake of liberation, for separation from these people is inevitable."
Having heard these words of his, the king trembled like a tree struck by an elephant;
taking him by his lotus-like joined palms, he spoke these words with a throat choked with tears: Bc_5.29 //
Withdraw this thought, my son, for this is not the time for you to take refuge in dharma;
they say that the practice of dharma has many defects when one is in the first stage of life and the mind is still fickle.

The mind of a youth whose senses are curious about sense-objects and whose resolve is incapable of enduring the hardships of vows wanders away from the forest, especially since he is unacquainted with solitude.

But for me, O lover of dharma, the time for dharma has come; having entrusted the royal splendor to you, who are its worthy vessel, O you of firm prowess, dharma exists through your valor. But if you were to abandon your father, it would become adharma.
Therefore, abandon this resolve; for now, be devoted to the duties of a householder.
For a man, having enjoyed the pleasures of youth, entry into the forest of asceticism is truly delightful.
Having heard these words of the king, he whose voice was like that of a sparrow replied:
"O King, if you will be my guarantor against four things, I shall not resort to the forest of asceticism."
May my life not be subject to death; may this health of mine remain free from disease;
may old age not seize my youth, and may misfortune not carry away this prosperity.
To his son, who had thus spoken of this difficult matter, the Śākya king addressed these words:
"Abandon this excessively persistent resolve; it is an object of ridicule, being both an overweening ambition and contrary to the proper order."
Then Meruguru spoke to his teacher: "If this course is not possible, I am not to be dissuaded;
for it is not right to hold back one who wishes to escape from a refuge that is being consumed by fire."
Since separation from the world is inevitable, surely it is better to separate oneself voluntarily;
for death will surely deprive me of my own purpose while I am still unfulfilled and against my will.
Having thus heard the resolve of his son who desired liberation, the lord of the earth said,
"He shall not go," and further provided for his protection and the most excellent objects of desire.
Then, having been duly instructed by his ministers out of great respect and affection according to the scriptures,
and having been forbidden by his father with tears, he entered his residence in deep sorrow.
He was gazed upon by women with tremulous eyes, like young does, whose faces were kissed by swaying earrings and whose breasts quivered with heavy sighs.
For he, as radiant as a mountain of gold, who intoxicates the hearts of excellent women,
captivated them with his ears, limbs, eyes, and physical form, as well as by the qualities of his speech, touch, and body.
Then, on the following day, blazing with his physical form like the sun,
he ascended the palace as if the rising sun were mounting Mount Meru, desiring to dispel the darkness with his own radiance.

Having ascended a magnificent golden throne, variegated with diamond inlays, which was like a tree of lamps blazing with the brilliance of gold and whose interior was filled with the incense of choice black aloe-wood, he took his seat.
Then, at night, excellent women attended upon that peerless youth, who was like Indra himself, with musical instruments;
just as throngs of apsarases attend the son of Draviṇendra upon the peak of Himavat, white as the moon.
Even with those supreme instruments resembling celestial lutes, he found neither delight nor joy;
for that virtuous man, desiring to go forth toward the bliss of the ultimate truth, took no pleasure in them.
Then, having perceived his resolve there, the gods of the Akaniṣṭha heaven, supreme in their ascetic power,
simultaneously induced sleep upon the women and caused their bodily movements to become distorted.
For there, one woman lay down, resting her cheek upon her trembling hand;
she had left behind her lute, which rested on her lap like a beloved wife adorned with golden plates, as if she were angry.
Another woman lay there, her white garment slipping from her breasts and her flute held in her hand;
she shone like a river whose banks laugh with foam, where lotuses are frequented by rows of straight bees.
Another woman slept embracing her mṛdaṅga drum as if it were her beloved, with her two arms— tender as the interior of a fresh lotus and joined by armlets as brilliant as refined gold.
Others, adorned with ornaments of fresh gold and wearing unsurpassed yellow garments,
fell down helplessly under the weight of deep sleep, like *karṇikāra* branches broken by an elephant.
Another lay leaning against the side of a window, her slender body bent like a bow;
with her beautiful necklace hanging down, she shone like a carved statue on a gateway.
The lotus-face of another woman, bent down with its decorative leaf-patterns bitten by her jeweled earrings,
shone like a hundred-petaled lotus with its stalk half-bent, stirred by a standing kāraṇḍava bird.
Others, lying down just as they had been sitting, their bodies bent low by the weight of their breasts,
shone as they embraced one another with the nooses of their arms adorned with golden bracelets.
And a certain woman, embracing a large lute as if it were a female friend, lay fast asleep;
with her golden strings trembling, she rolled about with a face radiant with earrings that had become disarrayed.

Another young woman, having loosened the beautiful cord from her arm and shoulder, lay down as if embracing her lover in the space between her thighs, weary from amorous play and full of graceful charm.
Others, though possessing large eyes and beautiful brows, had their eyes closed;
they were like lotus ponds whose buds have shrunk when the sun has set.
Another woman, her hair disheveled and loose, with her ornaments and the hem of her garment slipping from her hips,
lay with her necklaces scattered, like a statue of a woman broken by an elephant.

Others, however, helpless and stripped of shame—though possessed of fortitude and endowed with the excellence of their physical forms—lay there breathing heavily and violently; distorted and with their arms flung out, they yawned.
Others, with their ornaments and garlands cast aside, their garments disheveled and unfastened, lay unconscious;
with their white eyes wide open and motionless, they did not shine as they slept, appearing as if their life-breath had departed.
Another lay down with her mouth agape, her limbs swollen, saliva trickling from her mouth, and her private parts exposed;
as if reeling from intoxication, she did not shine, yet she maintained her distorted form.
Thus, that multitude of women, lying down in accordance with their respective natures and lineages,
bore a resemblance to a lake whose lotuses have been bent and broken by the wind.

Having observed those young women lying there in such various distorted postures with their unsteady movements— the prince, though possessed of a virtuous body and elegant speech, felt deep revulsion toward them.
In this world of living beings, such is the nature of women: impure and deformed.
Yet, deceived by garments and ornaments, a man conceives passion for the objects of women.

If a man were to reflect upon the true nature of women and such transformations as these seen in dreams, he would certainly not increase his heedlessness in this matter; yet, struck down by the mental construction of their virtues, he falls into passion.
Thus, having perceived that interval, the desire to depart at night arose within him;
then, the gods, understanding his mind, opened the door of the palace.
Then he descended from the roof of the palace, censuring those young women as they lay asleep;
having descended, he went forth without hesitation to the first courtyard of the house.
Having awakened his swift attendant Chandaka, he spoke to him thus:
"Bring the horse Kanthaka; I am in haste, for today I desire to depart from here to attain the deathless."

"The joy that has arisen in my heart today, and the resolve that has taken root in my mind—even in this solitude I feel as if I have a protector; surely the desired goal has come face to face with me."
"Having cast aside both modesty and deference, these young women lie before me as if they were naked;
and since the door-panels have opened of their own accord, it is surely now my time to depart. (Bc 5.70)
Then, having received his master’s command, although he already understood the king’s decree, he—
feeling as if impelled by another within his own mind— set his thoughts upon bringing back the horse.

Then he brought that excellent horse to his master— a horse whose mouth was adorned with a golden bit, whose back was covered with a soft bedding, and who was endowed with strength, courage, speed, and noble lineage.
With a tail-root like that of a falcon, with heels, a short mane, and ears set low upon his tail;
with a back, belly, and flanks that were alternately depressed and elevated, and with a broad muzzle, forehead, hips, and chest.
Embracing him, that broad-chested one comforted him with a lotus-like hand and commanded him with sweet-syllabled words, as if desiring to enter the midst of an army.
"O best of horses, it is said that many enemies have been defeated in battle by the king while mounted upon you; therefore, act in such a way that I too may duly attain the state of immortality."
Companions are indeed easy to find for a man in battle, in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, or in the acquisition of wealth;
but companions are difficult to find for one who has fallen into calamity or who seeks refuge in the Dharma.

And those who here become my companions in deeds that are either defiled or grounded in dharma— as my inner self understands it, those people will certainly partake in the consequences of such actions.
Having understood this departure of mine, which is endowed with righteousness, for the sake of the welfare of the world,
O best of horses, exert yourself with speed and prowess for your own benefit and for the benefit of the world.
Having thus instructed his noble steed as if he were a friend in a matter of duty, the best of men, desiring to go to the forest, ascended the white horse—
possessing a radiant body like the sun— and appeared like the sun mounting an autumnal cloud.
Then that noble steed, avoiding the harsh noise of the dead of night that would awaken the attendants,
went forth with his jaw-noises silenced and his neighing stilled, his paces broken and hurried by agitation.

Then the yakṣas, with bodies bent low, grasped his hooves with the tips of their hands— which resembled lotuses and whose forearms were adorned with golden bracelets— holding them as if they were lotus stalks, while moving with cautious steps.
Those city gates, which were closed by heavy crossbars and doors and could not easily be opened even by elephants,
became open of their own accord before the prince as he passed, their sounds silenced.

Having resolved his mind upon renunciation and become indifferent to all worldly concerns, he then departed from his father’s city, leaving behind his father who faced him, his young son, the devoted people, and supreme sovereignty.
Then he, whose eyes were like the petals of a stainless lotus, looked toward the city and let out a lion’s roar:
"Having not yet seen the further shore of birth and death, I shall not enter this city named Kapila."
Having heard these words of the Lord of Wealth, the members of his assembly rejoiced;
and the hosts of gods, their minds filled with joy, wished him success in his resolve to break his fast.
Perceiving his resolve, which was exceedingly difficult to accomplish, other gods, whose bodies were like fire,
created light upon the snowy path, like rays of the moon streaming through a rift in the clouds.
Like a horse following the lead of a bay steed, he, however, as if impelled by his own mind,
traversed many yojanas through the sky, which was filled with stars harsh with the glow of dawn.
Thus ends the fifth canto, named "The Great Departure," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.
Then, when the sun, the eye of the world, had risen for a mere moment,
that best of men beheld the hermitage of Bhārgava.
Seeing that [forest], where the deer slept in trust and the birds remained at ease,
he felt as if he had found rest and as if his purpose were fulfilled.
To dispel their astonishment, for the sake of asceticism and worship,
and to maintain his own self-restraint, he dismounted from the back of the horse.
Having dismounted, he touched the horse, saying, "It is crossed," and being filled with joy, he spoke to Chandaka as if bathing him with his eyes.
"O gentle one, by pursuing this horse with a speed like that of Tārkṣya,
you have demonstrated your devotion to me as well as your own prowess."
"In every way, even though I am occupied with other duties, I have been taken up by you in your heart; for such is this love for a husband, and such is your power."
One who is capable yet lacks affection exists; one who possesses devotion yet lacks capability also exists;
but one who is both devoted and capable, such as you, is rare indeed upon this earth.
I am pleased with this noble deed of yours,
for you possess this disposition toward me that turns away even from fruits.
Who would not be well-disposed toward a person who has attained success?
Even one's own kin mostly turn into strangers when misfortune occurs.
A son is maintained for the sake of the family; a father is served for the sake of support. The world clings out of expectation; there is no such thing as self-interest without a motive.
What need is there for many words? In brief, you have done me a very great kindness.
Return now, taking the horse; I have reached my desired goal.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed one, desiring to bestow his favor,
removed his ornaments and gave them to him whose mind was deeply distressed.
Taking from his crown a radiant jewel that performed the function of a lamp,
he stood uttering these words, like Mount Mandara with the sun upon it.
O Chanda, having bowed many times with this jewel, the king should be petitioned—
without losing his confidence— in order to bring an end to his distress.
I have entered this grove of asceticism for the purpose of destroying birth and death;
certainly not out of a thirst for heaven, nor from lack of affection, nor from anger.
Therefore, you should not grieve for me who have thus departed;
for even after a long time of union, we shall no longer exist through the power of time.
Since separation is inevitable, my mind is set upon liberation,
so that there may never again be a parting from my own kin.
You should not grieve for me, who have gone forth to abandon sorrow;
rather, it is the passionate ones, attached to desires which are the very causes of grief, who are to be pitied.
"And this, it is said, was our firm resolve from of old;
