thus, as I walk upon the path that has become my inheritance, I am not to be grieved for."
For upon the passing away of a man, those who inherit his wealth appear on this earth; but heirs to his Dharma are rare, or perhaps do not exist at all.
Even if it should be that he has gone to the forest at an improper time,
there is no such thing as an "improper time" for the Dharma when life is so fickle.
Therefore, my resolve is this: I must seek my own welfare this very day;
for what confidence can there be in life when death stands as an adversary?
O gentle one, you should inform the lord of the earth of these and other matters,
and you should strive in such a way that he does not even think of me again.
"You must speak of our lack of virtue to the king;
for through a lack of virtue, affection is abandoned, and once affection is abandoned, one is no longer mourned."
Having heard these words, Chanda, overwhelmed by grief,
replied with hands joined in reverence and a voice choked with tears:
"O Lord, because of this very state of yours which causes distress to your kinsmen,
my heart sinks like an elephant in the mud of a river."
Whose tears would this resolve of yours not provoke?
Even in a heart made of iron it would do so; how much more so in one overwhelmed by affection?
Where is this delicacy of yours, worthy indeed of a celestial palace bed,
and where is the ground of the ascetic grove, covered with sharp sprouts of darbha grass?
"But having heard of your resolve, O Lord, when this horse was brought by me,
it was by divine power alone that I was compelled to do so through force."
For how could I, being under my own control and knowing this resolve of yours,
lead the horse back to the sorrow of Kapilavastu?
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, you ought not to abandon this king, who is affectionate and aged and longs for his son, just as an atheist abandons the true Dharma.
And you ought not to forget that second mother, the queen, who was exhausted by the labors of raising you, just as an ungrateful person forgets a kindness received.

You ought not to abandon the queen— who has young sons, who conducts herself with virtue, who is the glory of her family, and who is devoted to her husband— just as a eunuch might abandon attained sovereignty.
You ought not to abandon your son, the praiseworthy Yaśodhara, the best among those who uphold fame and dharma; you should not forsake him as a man of vice abandons his supreme reputation.
Now that you have resolved to renounce both your kin and your kingdom, O Lord, it does not behove you to abandon me; for your feet are my only refuge.
With my heart burning with grief, I am not able to go to the city,
having abandoned you in the forest, just as Sumantra did for Rāghava.
For what indeed will the king say to me when I have returned to the city without you? Out of a desire to appear polite, what shall I say regarding your inner apartments?
As for what you said— that faults should be spoken of even in a king— what such non-existent fault could I possibly say of you, who are as blameless as a sage?
With a heart full of shame and a tongue faltering,
what that I might say— who indeed would be able to believe it?
O Knower of Faults, whoever would speak of or believe that the moon possesses sharpness, he would likewise speak of or believe that you possess faults.
For one who is ever compassionate and constantly sensitive to the suffering of others, the abandonment of those who are dear is not fitting; turn back and be gracious to me.

O Chanda, let this torment regarding my separation be abandoned;
for among embodied beings of various births, separation is indeed inevitable.
Even if I myself do not abandon my own kin out of affection,
death will inevitably cause us to forsake one another against our will.
Where am I now, and where is that mother of mine, whose efforts were rendered fruitless— she by whom I was held in the womb through great longing and sufferings?
Just as birds that have gathered at a tree depart once more,
so too the meeting of living beings necessarily ends in separation.
Just as clouds, having come together, disperse once more,
so too do I consider the union and separation of living beings.
Since this world departs, deceiving one another in succession,
it is therefore not fitting to harbor a sense of "mine" regarding a meeting that is like a dream.
Trees are separated from their innate leaf-color;
since the disjunction of one thing from another occurs, why should it not happen to me as well? (Bc 6.49)
This being so, do not grieve, gentle friend; you may go.
But if there is still affection remaining, return again even after you have gone.
And you should say to the people in Kapilavastu who have expectations for us:
"Let that affection be abandoned; let this [our] resolve be heard."
"Either he will surely come quickly after bringing about the end of birth and death,
or, failing to achieve his goal and lacking further effort, he will meet his end."
Having heard these words of his, Kanthaka, the best of steeds,
licked his feet with his tongue and shed warm tears.
With his webbed hand, marked with the svastika and featuring a wheel in its center,
the prince touched him and spoke like a companion.
"Release your tears, Kanthaka; you have demonstrated the nature of a noble horse.
Endure this, for soon this labor of yours will become fruitful."
Then that steadfast one, having taken from the hand of Chandaka the jeweled hilt and the sharp sword adorned with golden patterns, drew it from its scabbard like a venomous serpent from its hole.
Having pulled it out—blue as a lotus petal—he cut off the variegated crown together with the hair;
and as its silken streamers were scattered in the air, he cast it away like a swan into a lake.
Out of a desire for worship and out of great respect, the inhabitants of heaven seized that [hair] which had been cast away;
in heaven, the hosts of gods honored it according to tradition with divine and extraordinary offerings.
Having cast aside his ornaments and his wife-like finery, and having placed the royal turban upon his head,
that steadfast man, seeing a garment of bark marked with golden swans, desired it as his dwelling-robe.
Then a forest-dweller of pure disposition, wearing saffron robes, having understood his state of mind, approached him; that one born of the Śākya king addressed him: Bc_6.60.
"The saffron robe is auspicious, for it is the banner of the sages; this murderous bow is indeed not fitting for you.
Therefore, gentle sir, if you have no attachment to it, give it to me; take this [robe] instead."
The hunter said: "O granter of desires, having gained confidence through this [act], I slay deer for my pleasure;
but if it is for a purpose, O you who resemble Śakra, then indeed, accept this white garment and bring it to me."
Then, with great joy, he took the forest garment and cast off his linen cloth;
the hunter, however, assuming a divine form, took that white garment and departed for heaven.
Then the prince and the horse-herd were likewise amazed as he proceeded in that manner;
moreover, they immediately showed great respect for his forest-dweller's garment.

Then, having dismissed Chanda with tearful face, that Great-souled One, bearing the robes of the saffron-dyed ascetic and possessing the glory of his vows, went toward the hermitage like the moon, the king of stars, enveloped by the clouds of twilight.
Then, as his lord thus departed for the forest of asceticism, indifferent to the kingdom and clad in discolored garments,
the horseman raised his arms aloft, wailed aloud, and fell prostrate upon the earth.
Beholding him once more, he wept aloud, embracing Kanthaka the horse with both arms;
then, despairing and lamenting again and again, he went toward the city with his body, but not with his heart.
In one place he brooded, in another he lamented; in one place he stumbled, and in another he fell.
Thus, as he went along, overcome by devotion and distressed, he performed many involuntary actions on the road.
Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Turning Back of Chandaka," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.

Then, having dismissed the weeping Chanda, whose face was bathed in tears, Sarvārthasiddha— free from worldly attachment due to his longing for the forest— overwhelmed that hermitage with his physical splendor and entered it like a perfected being (*siddha*).
That prince, with the gait of a lion-king, entered that deer-park like a deer;
though deprived of royal splendor, he captivated the eyes of all those in the various stages of life by the splendor of his physical form.
For the wheel-bearers, together with their wives, stood still with their hands joined in reverence out of curiosity;
they gazed upon him who was like Indra but did not move forward, like draft-animals with their heads half-bowed.
The Brahmins, having gone outside for the sake of firewood, returned with fuel, flowers, and sacred grass in their hands;
though preeminent in asceticism and firm in resolve, they did not go to see him, nor did they enter his hermitage.
And seeing the cloud rising like a dark blue mountain, the peacocks, filled with joy, let out their cries;
and the deer with restless eyes, as well as those who roam among the wild beasts, abandoned the young grass and stood facing him.
Seeing that lamp of the Ikṣvāku clan, blazing like the rising sun,
the cows that yielded milk for the oblations, though already milked, felt a surge of joy and milk flowed forth once more.
"Could this be one of the Vasus, the eighth? Or perhaps one of the Ādityas who has descended?"—such words were uttered loudly by the sages there, born of wonder at the sight of him.
Like a second body of the Bull among the Gods, or like the light of the world of the moving and the unmoving,
he illuminated the entire forest, having descended by chance like the sun.
Then, having been duly honored and invited by those hermits, he, along with his retinue,
returned the honor to those upholders of the Dharma with a voice like a water-bearing cloud.

Desiring liberation, he wandered through that hermitage, which was crowded with people performing meritorious deeds out of a longing for heaven, while observing the various and wondrous ascetic practices.
Having observed the various manifestations of asceticism there in that penance grove belonging to those whose wealth is austerity, the gentle prince,
desiring to know the truth, spoke thus to a certain ascetic who was following him.
Since this was my first sight of a hermitage today, and because I do not know this rule of dharma,
you ought to explain to me the certainty regarding that for which you have set out.

Then that twice-born man, whose delight was in asceticism, gradually related to that bull among the Śākyas— whose stride was like that of a bull— the various distinctions of austerity and the fruit of ascetic practice.

Food that is not grown in a village, water-grown plants, water, fruit, and roots—this is the livelihood of sages according to the scriptures; however, those various distinctions of ascetic practices differ from one another.
Some live by gleaning like birds; some roam for grass like deer;
some coexist with serpents, having become like anthills through the forest wind.
Others, whose livelihoods were earned through labor involving stones, ate food crushed by their own teeth;
likewise, others, having cooked for the sake of others, performed their own tasks only if a remnant remained.
Some, with masses of matted hair drenched in water, offer oblations twice into the fire preceded by mantras;
others, having plunged into the waters along with fish, dwell there with bodies scarred by turtles.
By such supreme austerities accumulated over time, some go to heaven and others to the world of men;
for one attains happiness through a path of suffering, and they say that happiness is indeed the root of Dharma.

Having heard these and other words of that ascetic, the son of the Lord of Men, though he had not yet perceived the ultimate truth, was not fully satisfied; slowly, he spoke thus to himself: ityevamādi dvipadendravatsaḥ śrutvā vacastasya tapodhanasya / adṛṣṭatattvo 'pi na saṃtutoṣa / śanairidaṃ cātmagataṃ babhāṣe // Bc_7.19 //
Austerity is manifold and consists of suffering, and the fruit of austerity is primarily heaven;
all worlds are subject to transformation—indeed, this exertion for the stages of life is but trifling.
Those who, having abandoned beloved kin and sensory pleasures, practice self-restraint for the sake of heaven,
are indeed separated from their current bonds only to desire a far greater bondage once again.
He who, through bodily fatigues designated as "austerities," strives for activity for the sake of desire,
failing to examine the faults of cyclic existence, seeks only suffering by means of suffering.
Living beings are constantly terrified of death, yet they strive with effort for rebirth;
since death is certain as long as there is active existence, they remain submerged in that very state from which they are afraid.
For this purpose some enter into distress; others undergo toil for the sake of heaven;
and the world of living beings—miserable in its hopes, failing to achieve its goal—falls indeed into misfortune for the sake of pleasure.
Indeed, this effort is not at all to be censured when it abandons the inferior to pursue the superior;
rather, the wise should perform that task with equal exertion wherein there is no further need for action.
If bodily suffering here were dharma, then bodily pleasure would be adharma;
yet through dharma one obtains happiness in the next world, therefore it is adharma that bears fruit in this life, while dharma bears fruit in the future.
Since the body proceeds and also ceases to act under the influence of the mind, self-control belongs to the mind alone; therefore, apart from the mind, the body is like a piece of wood.
If merit is desired through purity of food, then even deer possess merit;
so too do those outsiders who, due to the fault of their destiny, have turned away from fruits.
If an intention regarding suffering is indeed a cause of merit, then surely that same intention should also be applied toward happiness.
If, however, there is no valid authority for an intention regarding happiness, then surely there is no authority for an intention regarding suffering either.

Likewise, those who, for the sake of purifying their karma, touch the water thinking it is a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), even there this mere satisfaction in the heart [is all they gain]; for water will not purify their sin.
If whatever water is touched by those possessed of virtue is considered a sacred ford on earth, then I regard virtues alone as the true ford; as for water, it is undoubtedly just water.
Thus he spoke, employing various arguments, and the sun went to its setting;
then he entered that forest, where the trees were discolored by the smoke of sacrificial offerings and which was tranquil through asceticism.
With the blazing *agnihotra* fires already lifted up, scattered with sages who had performed their ablutions,
and its divine shrines resonant with the sound of muttered prayers, it was like the active workshop of Dharma itself.
For some nights there, he who shone like the moon dwelt while observing their ascetic practices;
and having scrutinized all those penances and concluded them to be insufficient, he departed from that site of asceticism.

Then the hermits followed him, their minds captivated by the majesty of his form, as the great seers followed Dharma itself when it was being oppressed by barbarians in that land and was departing from the country.
Then he beheld those ascetics, rich in penance, sporting with their matted locks, bark garments, and rags;
and following after their austerities, he stayed at the foot of a beautiful and auspicious tree.

Then, having approached and surrounded that best of men, the hermitage-dwellers stood there; and the eldest among them, with great respect, spoke these words in a gentle and conciliatory tone: Bc_7.37.
When you arrived, this hermitage became as if full; when you depart, it becomes utterly empty.
Therefore, my dear son, you ought not to abandon it, just as one who wishes to live must not abandon his cherished life-force.
For nearby stands the holy mountain Himavat, frequented by Brahman-sages, royal sages, and celestial sages;
indeed, those very austerities of the ascetics whose wealth is penance flourish further through its proximity.
Likewise, the holy fords on all sides were like stairways to the vault of heaven,
frequented by righteous-souled self-controlled ones, as well as by celestial seers and great sages.
For this reason as well, it is more fitting for one who possesses the remainder of his dharma to serve the northern direction;
it is not fitting for a wise man to set foot even once toward the south.

"In this forest of asceticism, if you have seen anyone who is inactive, fallen into confused conduct, or impure—because of whom you have no desire to dwell here—then tell me; let your stay be as long as you please."
For these desire you, who resemble a treasury of asceticism, as a companion in their penance;
indeed, dwelling together with you, who are equal to Indra, would bring prosperity even to Bṛhaspati.
When this had been said, that foremost of the wise,
who had made a vow for the destruction of existence, declared his inner disposition amidst the ascetics by the chief of ascetics.
Because these sages, who uphold the Dharma and are upright in nature, treat guests with such affection as they would their own kin,
these various manifestations of feeling toward me have produced in me supreme joy and great honor.
In short, by these words—smooth, delightful, and heart-pleasing—I feel as if I have been bathed;
and now, the delight of me, a novice in the Dharma, has truly begun to stir once more.
To leave you who have thus engaged yourselves as protectors, showing such great partiality toward me, will cause me as much sorrow as it would for one abandoning his own kinsmen. (Bc 7.47)
"This dharma of yours leads to heaven, but my desire is for the state beyond rebirth;
it is for this reason that I have no wish to dwell in this forest, for the dharma of cessation has been separated from the dharma of worldly engagement."
It is not that I have no affection for you, nor is it due to any offense by others that I am departing from this forest;
for you all are established in the Dharma in accordance with the ancient age, and are indeed like great seers.
Then, having heard the prince’s words— which were truthful, meaningful, very gentle, powerful, and yet dignified— those ascetics felt a special degree of great respect.

There, however, a certain twice-born man—lying on ashes, tall, with a topknot, dressed in garments of bark, with reddish-brown eyes and a long, thin nose, and holding a water-pot in one hand—spoke these words: Bc_7.51.
O wise one, your resolve is indeed noble, you who, as a youth, have perceived the defects in birth;
for having properly deliberated upon both heaven and liberation, he whose mind is set on liberation is truly a man of worth.
For those possessed by passion desire to go to heaven through various sacrifices, austerities, and observances;
but those endowed with spiritual strength, having fought against passion as if against an enemy, seek liberation.
If this resolve of yours is firm, then go quickly to Vindhyakoṣṭha;
there dwells that sage Arāḍa, who has obtained the eye of insight regarding the ultimate good.
Therefore, you shall hear the path of reality and, provided there is a desire for it, you will practice it accordingly;
however, as I perceive it, this very mind of yours will likewise cast aside his [the Buddha's] wisdom.
With a prominent and elevated nose, large and long eyes,
copper-colored lower lips, and white, sharp fangs, and with a slender,
red tongue— this one shall indeed drink the entire ocean of all that is to be known.
Your profundity which is unfathomable, your radiance, and your marks—
thereby you shall attain a teachership on this earth such as was never attained even by the sages in former ages.
Then the prince, having greeted those sages with the words "Excellent!", departed;
and they too, having honored him according to the prescribed rites, entered the penance grove of the hermits.
Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Entrance into the Ascetic Grove," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.
Then that groom, dejected because his master had thus departed for the forest, made an effort on the road to restrain his grief; nevertheless, his tears would not be stayed.
The path which he had traveled with that horse by his master’s command in a single night,
he now traversed in eight days, reflecting upon the separation from his lord.
The horse Kanthaka, though adorned with ornaments as before, moved about with a dejected spirit; bereft of his master, he became listless and appeared as if his splendor had vanished.
Having turned back and facing toward the penance grove, he neighed piteously again and again;
though overcome by hunger on the road, he neither took pleasure in nor accepted grass or water, just as he had done before.
Then, deprived of that high-souled one whose very nature was the welfare of the world, they gradually approached the city named Kapila as if it were empty,
like the sky bereft of the sun.
Though adorned with waters graced by white lotuses and embellished by trees bearing flowers,
that very grove of his, resembling a forest, did not shine with the city-dwellers whose joy had departed.
Then, as if being extinguished by men wandering in every direction with dejected minds, lacking luster, and their eyes struck by tears,
those two slowly entered the city, which seemed as if it had been drained of its life.
And having observed that the two, whose bodies were drooping and who had departed without the bull of the Śākya clan,
the citizens shed tears along the road, as if the chariot of Daśaratha’s son had returned to the city.
Then, filled with indignation and their voices choked with tears, the people who had followed him on the road spoke thus and pursued Chandaka from behind, asking:
"Where is the prince, the joy of the city and the kingdom? He has been carried off by you!"
Then he said to those devoted people: "I did not abandon the prince;
rather, it was I who, weeping in the lonely forest, was sent away along with his householder's dress."
Having heard these words of his, those people reached the conclusion that it was indeed most difficult to achieve;
they held back the falling water of their tears rather than the water from their eyes, and they reproached their own minds for the fruitlessness of their efforts.
Then they said: "Let us enter that very forest today where he has gone, who possesses the prowess of the king of elephants;
for without him we have no desire to live, just as embodied beings have none when their senses have perished."
This city, abandoned by him, has become a forest; and that forest, joined with him, has become a city.
Indeed, without him, our city does not shine, just as heaven did not shine after the slaying of Vṛtra, being bereft of Indra.
Then, thinking that the prince had turned back, the women crowded to the rows of windows;
but seeing the horse with its back empty, they closed the windows again and wailed aloud.
Having undergone the initiatory rite for the sake of obtaining a son, the lord of men— his mind distressed by both his vow and his grief—
recited prayers in the temple of the god and performed various rites according to his desire.
Then, his eyes filled with tears, taking the horse and followed by the horse-attendants,
he entered the royal palace, struck down by grief as if his master had been led away by an enemy in battle.
And as he entered the palace of the lord of men, looking about with eyes streaming with tears,
Kanthaka let out a loud cry, as if announcing his sorrow to the people.
Then the birds dwelling within the palace grounds and the well-tended horses tethered nearby echoed the sound of that horse, suspecting the arrival of the prince.
And the people, deceived by an excess of joy as they stood near the inner apartments of the lord of men, thought:
"Surely the prince is entering, for this horse Kanthaka is neighing. (Buddhacarita 8.19)
Then, out of excessive joy yet fainting with grief, their eyes eager for a sight of the prince,
the women rushed forth from the palace in hope, like flickering flashes of lightning from an autumn cloud.
With disheveled hair, wearing soiled garments, and faces whose eyes were robbed of collyrium by tears,
the women did not shine, deprived of their ornaments like stars in the sky reddened at the end of the night.
With feet unadorned by anklets and not yet reddened by copper-colored lac; with faces lacking earrings and necks held upright;
with hips naturally full yet devoid of girdles; and with breasts as if robbed of their beauty, being without strings of pearls—(8.22).
Beholding Chandaka and the horse alone and without their protector, those excellent women, their eyes filled with tears and their faces dejected,
wept like cows abandoned by their bull in the midst of a forest.
Then Gautamī, the queen of the lord of the earth, filled with tears like a mother cow that has lost its calf,
threw her arms around him and fell down like a golden plantain tree with trembling leaves.
With their luster gone, their shoulders and arms drooping, the other women were as if deprived of consciousness by despair;
they neither cried out, nor shed tears, nor sighed, nor moved, but remained standing like figures in a painting.

Other women, fainting from grief for their husband, drenched their breasts—which had been rubbed with sandalwood paste—with the streams flowing from their eyes; they were like rocks being drenched by waterfalls.
And with their faces drenched by the water from their eyes, that royal palace then shone like a lake whose lotuses are dripping with water,
struck by the rain of clouds during the season of new waters.

With hands that were well-rounded, plump-fingered, closely set, unadorned, and with hidden veins— hands like lotuses— the beautiful women struck their breasts, like wind-swayed creepers striking themselves with their own sprouts.
And yet those women shone with their high breasts heaving together as they trembled from the blow of his hand,
like rivers with pairs of *rathāṅga* birds shaking as they are tossed by the forest wind.
Just as they pressed their chests with their hands, so too did they press their hands with their chests;
there, the women, indifferent to compassion, caused mutual pain by means of the tips of their hands and their breasts.
Then Yaśodharā, her eyes reddened with rage, her breasts heaving with sighs, and bearing a stream of tears born of deep sorrow, spoke in a voice faltering and choked with the bitterness of despair:

Yaśodharā, her eyes reddened with wrath, her voice faltering and choked with the bitterness of despondency, and her breasts trembling with sighs, spoke while shedding a torrent of tears born of profound grief.
"O Chandaka, where has he gone—he who was the fulfillment of my heart's desire—who left me behind while I lay fast asleep and helpless in the night?
Now that you have returned with Kanthaka, as these three have all departed together, my mind trembles."
"Having committed this ignoble, unkind, and hostile act toward me, O cruel one, why do you weep here today?
Restrain your tears and be of a contented mind; for your tears do not correspond to that deed of yours."
Accompanied by you—a beloved, submissive, beneficial, virtuous, and effective companion—the noble son has departed never to return; rejoice, for by good fortune your toil has borne fruit.
Better for a man is a discerning enemy than a foolish friend who is unskilled in proper conduct;
for by you, speaking as a friend yet lacking wisdom, a great calamity has been brought upon this family.
For these women are indeed pitiable, their ornaments cast off, their red eyes turbid with clinging tears;
though their husband stands by, equal to the earth of the Himavat mountains, they have lost their splendor like widows.
And these rows of palaces, with their balconies and railings tilted and the long cooing of pigeons clinging to them,
seem to weep bitterly, now separated from him and his womenfolk.
This horse Kanthaka, too, must certainly have been intent on doing harm to these people in every way;
for he has carried away my everything from here while the people were fast asleep at night, like a thief of jewels.
When he was indeed capable of enduring even the blows of incoming arrows, let alone the strokes of a whip;
how then has he gone away out of fear of the lash’s fall, taking with him both my fortune and my heart alike?
Today this ignoble creature neighs loudly, as if filling the very palace of the king;
yet when it was carrying away my beloved, that lowest of horses remained utterly silent.
For had he neighed, awakening the people, or had he made a sound with his hooves upon the earth,
or had he produced a great noise with his jaws, this sorrow of mine would not have come to pass.

Having thus heard these words of the Goddess, which were based on her lamentation and whose syllables were choked by tears, Chandaka, with downcast face, his voice faltering with sobs, and palms joined in reverence, slowly uttered this reply: Bc_8.42.
O Queen, you ought not to reproach Kaṇṭhaka, nor should you harbor anger toward me;
know that we are both entirely without fault, for that god among men has departed like a god, O Queen.
For although I was aware of the royal decree, as if compelled by certain deities,
I quickly brought this horse and likewise followed it on the road without experiencing any fatigue.
Even this excellent steed, as he went, did not touch the earth with the tips of his hooves, which seemed held aloft as if by some divine power;
likewise, with his face restrained as if by fate, he made no sound with his jaws nor did he neigh.
When the prince went outside, the gate opened of its own accord;
and the nocturnal darkness was rent asunder by him as if by the sun. Let this too be understood as a divine ordinance of his ascetic merit.

Although thousands of people in the palace and the city remained vigilant by the king’s command, they were not aware of it at that time, being overcome by sleep; therefore, let it be understood that this was the work of destiny.

Since at this time the garment appropriate for dwelling in the forest was bestowed upon him by a celestial being, and that crown which had been cast away in heaven was worn by him— therefore, let it be understood that this too is the work of destiny.
Therefore, O Queen, you ought not to blame us for his departure;
it was neither my own will nor that of this horse. For he went forth, escorted by the gods.

Having thus heard of that wondrous departure of the Great-souled One, accompanied by many gods, those women were filled with amazement as if their grief had vanished; yet, they experienced the fever of longing because of his renunciation.

Then Gautamī, her eyes overwhelmed with despair, like a female osprey distressed by the loss of its young, abandoned her fortitude; she wailed aloud, fainted, and with a tear-stained face, she spoke: Bc_8.51.
His hair was wavy, soft, dark, and beautiful; growing from distinct roots, it rose up and spread over the earth, fit to serve as a circlet for the crown of a king.
With long arms, the prowess of a lion-king, eyes like those of a great bull, and a radiance as brilliant as gold;
with a broad chest and a voice like the deep roll of a drum—one such as this deserves to dwell in a hermitage.
Surely this earth is unfortunate, for she has lost that husband of noble deeds and unsurpassed merit;
for such a virtuous king as he is born only through the merits and good fortune of his subjects.

How indeed will those two feet— with fingers webbed with beautiful lines, soft, with hidden ankles, as tender as lotus flowers, and marked with the wheel in their centers— tread upon the hard ground at the edge of the forest?

How indeed will that vigorous body, accustomed to couches and seats upon the roof of a celestial palace, and honored with costly garments, agallochum, and sandalwood, endure in the forest when cold, heat, and rain arrive?
Proud of his lineage, his being, his strength, his splendor, his learning, his fortune, and his youth, he was accustomed only to giving and not to begging; how will he wander for alms from others?

Having slept upon a pure bed of gold, being awakened at night by the sounds of musical instruments— alas, how will he, now observing his vow, sleep today upon the bare ground covered only by a portion of a single cotton cloth?
Hearing this piteous lamentation, those women embraced one another with their arms and shed tears from their eyes, like creepers shaken by the wind dropping honey from their flowers.
Then Yaśodharā fell to the ground like a female ruddy goose separated from her mate;
distressed, she lamented softly here and there, her voice repeatedly choked by sobs.
If he wishes to practice dharma while abandoning me, his helpless partner in dharma, where is his dharma?
For how can he who desires to enjoy ascetic toil be said to possess dharma without a partner in dharma?
He surely does not hear of his ancestors, the former kings beginning with Mahāsudarśa, who retired to the forests together with their wives; for he desires to practice the Dharma without me.

Or, in sacrifices consecrated by Vedic injunctions, he does not see both husband and wife as initiated; they both desire to enjoy the fruit equally even in the hereafter. Therefore, envy for my merit has arisen in him.

Surely that lover of dharma, knowing our mutual quarrels of mind born from jealousy and affection, has grown weary of me, his angry wife; and now, fearing nothing, he desires to seize the apsarases in the world of Mahendra, having abandoned me.

But this is my reflection: what kind of excellence of form do those women there possess, for whose sake he performs austerities in the forest, having abandoned both sovereignty and even his devotion to me?
Truly, I have no longing for the happiness of heaven, nor is that difficult to attain even for a self-possessed person;
rather, my heart's desire is this: how might he, who is dear to me, not abandon me either in this world or in the next?
If I am so unfortunate as not to behold the face of my husband— long-eyed and bright with a pure smile—
then even this ill-fated Rāhula shall never again roll about upon his father’s lap.

Alas! How cruel and most terrible is the mind of that wise one, who, possessing a delicate complexion, yet alas, abandons such an infant son—a child whose sweet prattle would bring joy even to an enemy! (Bca 8.68)
Surely my heart is most cruel, made either of stone or even of iron,
since it does not shatter when my husband— who was accustomed to comfort— has gone to the forest, left like one who is helpless and bereft of fortune.
Thus here the queen, fainting from grief for her husband, wept, brooded, and lamented repeatedly;
for though she was by nature steadfast, in her sorrow that virtuous woman remembered neither fortitude nor shame.
Then, beholding Yaśodharā thus prostrate upon the earth, overwhelmed by her lamentations of grief,
the women cried out with tearful faces like great lotuses struck by rain.
Having completed his recitation and performed the auspicious fire-offerings, the king emerged from the temple;
struck by the distressed cries of the people, he trembled like an elephant at the sound of a thunderbolt.
Having observed both Chandaka and Kanthaka, and having heard the firm resolve of his son,
the lord of the earth, struck down by grief, fell like the banner of Indra at the conclusion of a festival.
Then, for a moment, deluded by grief for his son and supported by people of equal birth, the king, standing upon the ground, gazed at the horse with eyes full of tears and lamented: *Bc_8.74*

O Kaṇṭhaka, after you had performed many deeds pleasing to me in battle, you have now done me a great injury; for by you, my beloved who is fond of virtue, was he whom I love sent away to the forest like one who is unloved, even though he himself is dear to me.
Therefore, either lead me today to where he is, or go quickly and bring him back here;
for without him, there is no life for me, just as there is none for one deeply afflicted by disease who lacks the proper medicine.

When Suvarṇaniṣṭhīvin was carried off by death, Saṃjaya performed what was most difficult to do: he did not die. But I, though my son who delighted in the Dharma has departed, am like one lacking self-mastery, seeking to release myself from life.

How indeed could even the mind of Manu—the lord of ten clans, the progenitor, the knower of the higher and the lower, whose very self was Vivasvat—not be bewildered when separated from his beloved and virtuous son? (Bc 8.78)
I envy that wise king, the son of King Aja and friend of Indra, who, when his son had departed for the forest, ascended to heaven; he did not live a miserable life with futile tears.
Tell me, O blessed one, of that hermitage courtyard where you have taken my water-offering;
for these vital breaths of mine, desiring to reach the state of the departed, long for it as they thirst.
Thus, casting aside his innate fortitude— which was like the earth itself— born as it was from the sorrow of separation from his son,
the king, overcome by grief for Rāma, lamented profusely like Daśaratha, nearly deprived of consciousness.

Then the counselor Matisaciva, endowed with the virtues of learning and discipline, and the elderly family priest spoke these words to him in a composed manner, exactly as was appropriate; neither with downcast faces nor yet devoid of sorrow.
"Abandon your grief, O best of men; come to steadfastness. You ought not, O wise one, to shed tears like one of weak resolve.
For many kings on this earth, having cast aside royal splendor like a crushed garland, have fled to the forests."

Moreover, this disposition of his is certain; remember the words of the seer Asita from long ago: for he cannot be made to dwell happily, even for a moment, in heaven or in the sovereignty of a universal monarch.
But if, O best of men, effort must indeed be made, then speak quickly so that we may go there;
let there be many kinds of battle here between your son and each of those various [opponents].
Then the lord of men commanded them: "Therefore, depart from here quickly;
for my heart finds no peace, like that of a forest bird longing for its young."
By the king’s command, "It is done," those two, the minister and the domestic priest, departed for that forest;
and the king also, together with his wives and the women of the harem, performed the remaining duties.
Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "The Lamentation in the Inner Apartments," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.
Then, spurred by the king with the goad of his tears, the minister and the priest,
like two noble steeds pierced by a whip, proceeded with all their effort swiftly toward that forest out of their affection for him.
Having reached that hermitage at the proper time, the two of them, weary from their journey and accompanied by a suitable retinue,
cast aside royal splendor and, with humble deportment, approached the very abode of Bhārgava.

Having honored that brahmin according to custom, and having been honored by him in a fitting manner, the two took their seats; then, after cutting short the conversation with the descendant of Bhṛgu who was seated upon his throne, they spoke of their own business.

"May your lordship consider this person as one who has studied under a king of pure vigor and pure, far-reaching fame, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, for the purpose of grasping the sacred scriptures and mastering the mantras."

To him, who was like Indra, there was a son like Jayanta; desiring to cross over the fear of old age and death, he has indeed come forth here for that purpose. May the Blessed One understand that we two have approached for his sake.
He said to them: "That long-armed prince has indeed arrived, yet he has not yet awakened.
Realizing that this dharma leads back to rebirth, he has set out with haste toward Arāḍa, seeking liberation."
Therefore, having perceived the truth from him and having taken leave of that brahmin, they immediately set out at once—
though weary, appearing as if unwearied through their devotion to the King— to the place where he had gone.
As they proceeded, the two of them saw him, radiant in his physical form despite being devoid of grooming,
seated by the roadside at the foot of a tree like the orb of the sun entered into a mass of clouds.
Then, leaving the carriage, the family priest approached him together with the mantra-master,
just as the sage Ātreya, accompanied by Vāmadeva, went to see Rāma while he was dwelling in the forest.
They both worshipped that Arhat, as Śukra and Aṅgiras worship Mahendra in heaven;
and he in turn honored those two Arhats, as Mahendra honors Śukra and Aṅgiras in heaven.
Having received permission from all sides, the two sat down on either side of the banner of the Śākya clan;
in his presence, they shone like the two Punarvasu stars in conjunction with the moon.
To that prince, who was seated at the foot of the tree and blazing with splendor, the family priest spoke,
just as Bṛhaspati spoke to Jayanta, the son of Śakra, when he was seated upon the Pārijāta tree in heaven.

O Prince, when the arrow of grief for you had plunged into his heart, the king fell into a swoon upon the ground for a moment; listen now to what he said to you as he shed a rain of tears from his eyes.
I know your resolve regarding the Dharma; I foresee this future destiny of yours.
Yet, because of your resorting to the forest at an untimely hour, I am consumed by a fire of grief that is like a blazing flame.
Therefore come, O lover of the Dharma; for my sake and for the sake of the Dharma itself, abandon this resolve.
For this torrent of grief strikes me down, just as the current of a river strikes its bank when it has swollen.
For just as the wind, the sun, fire, and the great thunderbolt act upon clouds, water, dry grass, and mountains,
so does grief act upon us by means of tearing, withering, burning, and shattering.
Therefore, enjoy this sovereignty over the earth for now; you shall go to the forest at the time prescribed by the scriptures.
Show consideration for me, your unwelcome kinsman, for compassion toward all beings is indeed the Dharma.
This dharma is not accomplished only in the forest; for ascetics, success is certain even in the city.
In this matter, wisdom and effort are the causes; for the forest and the [ascetic] marks are merely the signs of the timid.

Even by householders—kings wearing crowns, with necklaces clinging to their chests and bracelets fixed upon their arms—moving within the lap of Fortune, the dharma of liberation was attained. (Bca 9.19)
The two younger brothers of Dhruva, namely Bali and Vajrabāhu; Vaibhrāja, Āṣāḍha, and Antideva;
likewise Janaka, the king of Videha, as well as Śālvadruma and King Senajit.
Know these kings to be householders disciplined in the dharma that leads to the supreme good;
therefore, O King, enjoy both simultaneously: sovereignty over the mind and royal splendor.
For I desire to enter the forest with that same joy, beholding you after you have been consecrated, while you are still wet from the water, closely embraced and holding the royal parasol.

"Thus the lord of the earth spoke to you with words whose syllables were choked with tears; having heard this, for the sake of his welfare, you ought out of affection to respond with your own affection. (Buddhacarita 9.23)
For the King of the Śākyas is sinking in a bottomless ocean of sorrow, a sea of suffering originating from you;
therefore, rescue him who is without a protector and without refuge, like a ship rescuing one submerged in the ocean.

Having heard that Bhīṣma, born from the womb of the Gaṅgā, and Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, performed their deeds for the sake of pleasing their fathers, you too ought to do what is desired by your father.
Recognize the queen, your nurtress, who has not yet departed toward the quarter favored by Agastya;
she is like a loving cow whose calf has been lost—perpetually distressed, weeping piteously and mournfully.
Like a female swan separated from her mate, like a female elephant abandoned in the forest by her bull,
you ought to rescue this bride with your very sight— she who, though possessing a protector, is now left without one.

Deliver that one son, Rāhula— who, though undeserving of suffering, bears within him the anguish of grief for his kin— from the sorrow of his relatives, just as the full moon is released from the eclipse of Rāhu.
The inner apartments and the entire city, being consumed by the fire of grief— with your absence as its fuel, sighs as its smoke, and darkness as its flame— long for the water of the sight of you.

Having heard those words of his domestic priest, that Bodhisattva—whose being was fully perfected and who knew the qualities of the virtuous—reflected for a moment and spoke this humble reply: sa bodhisattvaḥ paripūrṇasattvaḥ śrutvā vacastasya purohitasya / dhyātvā muhūrtaṃ guṇavadguṇajñaḥ pratyuttaraṃ praśritamityuvāca // Bc_9.30 //
I recognize the affection parents have for their offspring, especially that which the king bears toward me;
yet, though I know this, being terrified of disease, old age, and calamity, I am forced by necessity to abandon my own kin.
Who indeed would not wish to see their own dear kinsman, were it not for the fact that there is ultimately separation from the beloved?
Since separation must occur even after a long time together, I therefore abandon even this heavy and painful body.
As for the grief you say the lord of men feels on my account, that is not pleasing to me;
for one suffers when there is separation from those who, like dream-visions, have come together.
And thus let your intellect reach this certainty after observing the manifold course of the world:
neither son nor kinsman is the cause of suffering; this affliction has its origin solely in ignorance.
Just as for travelers who have met here on this road, separation is inevitable in time;
what wise person, then, would indulge in grief when deprived of those people designated as kinsmen? (Bc 9.35)
Having left his own kin here, he deceives others in the next world, and then returns here once more;
having gone there, he goes yet elsewhere. Since people depart in this manner, what cause for attachment is there?
Since death has been active for my destruction in every state of existence from the very moment of conception,
why has your honor, who loves his son, told me to take refuge in the forest at this improper time?
There is an improper time for the pursuit of sense objects, and likewise, the right time is prescribed for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
Time drags away the entire world through all its seasons; yet, there is no such time that can obstruct the supreme good when it is being carried out.
That noble kingdom which the king desires to bestow upon me, wishing to be free from it himself, is indeed worthy of his father;
yet it is not fit for me to accept out of greed, just as unwholesome food is not for a sick man.
How indeed can it be fitting for a wise man to enter into kingship, which is a source of delusion,
wherein there is agitation, intoxication, exhaustion, and the oppression of dharma through the misconduct of others?

For a kingdom is like a palace of Jāmbūnada gold that is ablaze, like exquisite food mixed with poison, or like a lotus pond infested with crocodiles; it is both delightful and a refuge for calamities.
And thus, neither sovereignty nor dharma brings happiness as they did for the kings of old who were filled with revulsion;
having abandoned their kingdoms in the height of their youth when suffering was unavoidable, they departed for the forest alone.
For it is better to eat grass in the forest, embracing supreme contentment as if it were a jewel,
and to dwell together with the misfortunes that easily beset prosperity, which are like invisible black snakes.
For it is indeed praiseworthy for kings to abandon their kingdoms and enter the forest out of a desire for dharma;
but it is not fitting for one who has broken his vow to leave the forest and enter the home again.
For what man of spirit, born into a noble family and having entered the forest out of a longing for the Dharma,
would cast off the saffron robe and, devoid of shame, take refuge even in the city of Indra?
For just as one who might, out of greed, delusion, or fear, take back food that he has already vomited up,
so too might one, out of greed, delusion, or fear, take back the desires he has renounced.
And he who, having somehow escaped from a burning house, should enter it once again—that man, having seen its faults, would out of delusion desire to take up household life once more. (Bc 9.47)
As for the tradition that kings attained liberation while remaining householders, this is not so;
for where is the Dharma of Liberation, which is characterized by tranquility, and where is the Dharma of Kingship, which is characterized by the rod of punishment?
If there is delight in tranquility, the kingdom is neglected; if the mind is fixed on the kingdom, tranquility is destroyed.
For tranquility and sharpness are incompatible, like the coexistence of cold and heat, or water and fire.
Either because of their certainty in that [truth], those lords of the earth abandoned their kingdoms and attained peace;
or else, though still possessing their kingdoms, they—because their senses were restrained—conceived the pride of having achieved liberation in that which was not final.
And let there be peace in their kingdom as is fitting; I have not come to the forest out of indecision.
For having cut the snare known as home and kin, I am liberated and do not wish to enter it again.

Having heard these words spoken by the prince—consonant with his own knowledge of the self, free from desire, logical, and powerful—the master of spells also gave this reply: ityātmavijñānaguṇānurūpaṃ muktaspṛhaṃ hetumadūrjitaṃ ca / śrutvā narendrātmajamuktavantaṃ pratyuttaraṃ mantradharo 'pyuvāca // Bc_9.52 //
This resolve of yours regarding the practice of Dharma is neither improper nor unjust; however, it is not timely.
For, having caused your father—who is in the prime of his life—to fall into grief, it would not be Dharma for you who desire Dharma.
Surely your intellect is not very subtle, or perhaps it is unskilled in the matters of dharma, artha, and kāma,
since you depart disregarding a visible benefit for the sake of a result whose cause remains unseen.
Some say that there is rebirth, while others, firm in their resolve, say there is none;
since this matter is thus a subject of doubt, it is fitting to enjoy the prosperity that has presented itself.
If there is some further activity, we shall delight therein according to its occurrence;
but if there is no further activity whatsoever, then upon the establishment [of reality], liberation from this world comes without effort.
Some say that there is a future world, yet they do not describe the means to liberation;
for they claim that nature is inherent in activity, just as heat is in fire and fluidity is in water.
Some describe both the auspicious and the inauspicious, as well as existence and non-existence, as arising from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since all this is inherent by its very nature, for that reason also, human effort is futile.

That the activity of the senses is fixed, as is the pleasantness or unpleasantness of objects, and that one is joined with old age and afflictions—what effort can there be in this? Is it not indeed their very nature?
Fire is extinguished by water, and the waters dry up through heat;
the elements, though distinct while residing within the body, attain unity and thus sustain the world.
That the state of being in the womb proceeds from the hands, feet, belly, back, and head;
and that the union of the self with that [body] occurs—those who know the truth declare this to be natural.
Who creates the sharpness of the thorn, or the diverse nature of beasts and birds?
All this proceeds from its own inherent nature; there is no exercise of will, so how could there be effort?

Others say that creation proceeds from Īśvara; in that case, what purpose does the Puruṣa have? That very cause which is determined for the engagement of the world is itself the cause for its cessation.
Some say that both the manifestation [of existence] and the destruction of existence have the self as their cause;
they proclaim that manifestation occurs without effort, whereas the attainment of liberation occurs through effort.
A man becomes free from debt to his ancestors through progeny, to the seers through the Vedas, and to the gods through sacrifices;
for him who is born together with these three debts, there is indeed liberation.
Thus, by this sequence of methods, those who know the truth declare liberation for one who exerts effort;
for even those seeking liberation, though they strive with vigor, encounter exhaustion through mere physical exertion.
Therefore, gentle friend, if you have devotion to liberation, follow the prescribed method according to the rules;
in this way, there will be the attainment of this goal and the destruction of the king’s anguish.

And as for this inclination of yours to enter a palace from the ascetic groves out of a sense of its defects—even there, my dear son, let no such anxiety arise; for even those of old went from the forests to their own homes.
Even while dwelling in the forest of asceticism, King Ambarīṣa returned to his city surrounded by his subjects;
likewise, Rāma, having come from the forest of asceticism, protected the earth when it was oppressed by the ignoble.
In the same way, the lord of Śālva named Druma returned from the forest with his army to the city;
and Antideva, the son of Saṃkṛti, having become a Brahman-sage through the venerable Vasiṣṭha, attained royal splendor.
Those who were thus kindled by the glory of the Dharma left the forests and entered dwellings;
therefore, there is no fault in returning home from the penance grove for the very sake of the Dharma.

Then, having heard those words of the minister— which were pleasing and beneficial to the king who was his very eye— the prince, established in fortitude, spoke these words, which were complete, orderly, unhindered, and measured.
"Whether this exists here or does not exist—this doubt of mine cannot be resolved by the words of another.
Having realized the truth through austerity and tranquility, I shall myself grasp that which is certain in this matter. (Bc 9.73)
It is not fitting for me to accept a view born of doubt, which is indistinct and mutually contradictory.
For what wise person would proceed on the strength of another's conviction, like a blind man in the dark following a blind guide?
Although I have not yet perceived the ultimate reality, my mind wavers between good and evil;
yet it is better for one of virtuous nature to suffer in vain than for one of censurable nature to find happiness even in the truth.
But seeing that this scripture is inconsistent, know that whatever has been spoken by the authoritative ones is correct;
understand that their authority consists in the fact that they have abandoned all faults, for one whose faults are abandoned will not speak untruth.
As for what you have said regarding my return home, citing examples such as Rāma and others—
those are not authoritative for you, for those whose vows are impaired are no longer sufficient as authorities for the determination of Dharma.
Even if the sun were thus to fall to the earth, or even if the Himalayan mountain were to lose its stability,
a common man who has not seen reality and whose senses are turned toward sense-objects would never again resort to the home life.
"I would enter a blazing fire, but I would not enter my home until my purpose was accomplished"—thus the proud man made his vow; then, rising as he pleased, he departed free from attachment.

Then, having heard his firm resolve, both the minister and the brahmin, with tearful faces and heavy hearts, followed him for a short distance; then, out of necessity, they slowly returned to the city.
Then, out of affection for him and devotion to the king, the two of them moved forward and stood still with longing;
for they were unable to look upon him on the road—he who was as invincible as the sun and radiant with his own splendor—nor could they bear to leave him.

Having appointed pure spies to move about in disguise in order to ascertain the movements of that man of supreme destiny, they departed with some difficulty, thinking, "How shall we go and see the king who is so longing for his beloved son? (Buddhacarita 9.82)
Thus ends the ninth canto, titled "The Search for the Prince," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.
That prince, broad-chested and powerful, having left behind those two officials in charge of the sacrificial offerings and mantras,
crossed the Ganges with its surging waves and went to the glorious city of Rājagṛha.
Well-guarded by mountains, adorned and supported by auspicious ascetics,
he reached the city marked by five peaks, as tranquil as the Self-Existent One reaching the summit of heaven.
Beholding his profundity and vigor, and his radiant body that surpassed all men,
the people there were then struck with wonder, as if they were looking upon the bull-bannered god Śiva himself observing the vow of Sthāṇu.
Seeing him, he who had gone by another way stood still; he who was standing on the path followed after;
he who had been going swiftly moved slowly; and whoever was sitting there sprang up.
Some person honored him with both hands; some paid homage by bowing their heads;
some greeted him with affectionate words; and some departed without having offered him any salutation at all.
Seeing him, those dressed in various garbs were struck with shame; their scattered chatter fell silent on the road.
In the very presence of Dharma as it were, not a single person harbored an unjust thought.
Even while engaged in other activities on the royal road, the gaze of women or men, fixed with great reverence upon that son of a king who was like a god, could not be satiated.
Whether it was his eyebrows, forehead, face, or eyes; his body, hands, or feet;
or his gait—whichever part of him anyone beheld there, their gaze became fixed upon that very spot.
And having seen him— with his brow marked by a tuft of hair, his long eyes, his radiant body, and his hands with auspicious webbing—
that splendor of Rājagṛha, which was worthy of protecting the earth, was deeply agitated upon seeing him in the garb of a monk.
Then Śreṇya, the lord of the courtyard of Magadha, beheld from his outer palace a vast multitude of people and asked the reason for it; thereupon, a man explained it to him.
"He who was told by the brahmins that he would attain either supreme knowledge or the sovereignty of the earth—
that very son of the Lord of the Śākyas is now seen by the people as one who has gone forth into homelessness."
Then the king, having heard the matter and having reached a firm conviction in his mind, spoke to that very man:
"Let it be known where he is going. Saying "So be it," the man then followed after him.
With eyes steady and looking only a yoke’s length ahead, his speech ceased and his gait restrained and slow,
that best of monks went for alms, having stilled both his limbs and his flickering mind.
Having taken whatever alms were obtained as they came, he went to a secluded mountain spring;
having consumed that there according to the proper rule, he ascended Mount Pāṇḍava.
In that boat, which was sheltered by a grove of *lodhra* trees and whose bowers were filled with the cries of peacocks, he,
clothed in saffron robes, shone like the young sun above the eastern mountain.
Seeing him there, that royal servant informed King Śreṇya;
and having heard this, the king set out for that place with a modest retinue out of great respect for him.
He, whose valor was equal to that of the Pāṇḍavas, whose stature was like a mountain,
who wore a crown, who moved with the gait of a lion, and who was a lion among men, ascended the best of mountains, the Pāṇḍava, like a lion with a flowing mane.
Then, upon its peak, he beheld the Bodhisattva, whose senses were stilled, appearing like a summit;
seated cross-legged, he was radiant like the rising moon emerging from a thicket of clouds.

Filled with wonder and humble, the lord of men approached him— who, by virtue of his physical splendor and tranquility, sat like an emanation of Dharma— just as Śakra approaches the Self-Existent One (Brahmā).
Approaching that foremost of those who know the path according to reason, he asked about his physical well-being;
and he, in turn, with a fitting gentleness, spoke to the king regarding his mental composure and freedom from ailment.
Then the king sat down upon a clean stone surface, blue as an elephant’s ear;
and having sat near him with his permission, desiring to know his state of mind, he spoke as follows:
I have the highest affection for your family, which has been inherited through tradition and well-tested;
since a desire to speak has arisen within me regarding my own age, therefore listen to these words of affection.
Your lineage is vast, beginning with the Sun; your youth is fresh, and this body of yours is radiant.
Why, then, has your mind turned so prematurely toward the life of a mendicant, and not toward sovereignty?
For this body of yours is worthy of red sandalwood paste, not fit for contact with saffron robes;
this hand is suited for protecting subjects, and it is not fit to eat food given by others.
Therefore, gentle friend, if you do not desire through force that kingdom which is your paternal inheritance out of affection for your father,
and if your mind is not inclined to tolerate his succession, then quickly enjoy half of this realm from me.
For in this way, there would be no oppression of one's own kin, nor would prosperity, which rests upon tranquility, perish even with the passage of time.
Therefore, show me your favor; for the success of the virtuous is augmented by association with the virtuous.
But rather, because of your pride in your lineage, you have no quality of trust toward us;
therefore, plunging into the arrayed armies with me as your ally, seek to conquer the enemies with your arrows.
Therefore, choose one of these according to your own judgment, and pursue virtue, wealth, and pleasure in accordance with the prescribed rules;
for by neglecting this triad of aims here through passion and the like, people meet with ruin both in this world and after death.
For that desire which comes at the expense of wealth and virtue, and that wealth which treats both virtue and desire with contempt—
should one’s desired wealth be such that it necessitates the abandonment of virtue by the cessation of both desire and wealth, then all of it should be relinquished.
Therefore, by pursuing the threefold set of goals, make this form of yours fruitful;
for they say that the complete attainment of virtue, wealth, and pleasure constitutes the full human purpose for men.
"You ought not to let these two thick arms, fit for drawing a bow, remain fruitless;
for like Māndhātṛ, they are capable of conquering even the three worlds here, let alone the earth. (Bc 10.31)
Indeed, I say this out of affection, not out of a passion for power nor out of wonder;
for seeing this mendicant’s garb of yours, compassion has arisen within me and tears have come to my eyes. (Bc 10.32)

As long as old age has not come upon you, overwhelming this form that is so worthy of your own lineage, enjoy these desires, O seeker of the mendicant’s life; for in due time, O lover of dharma, you shall practice the dharma.
Indeed, one who is aged is able to attain the Dharma, for old age finds no place in the enjoyment of desires;
therefore, they say that desires are for the young, wealth for the middle-aged, and the Dharma for the elderly.
In this world of living beings, periods of youth are indeed adversaries to both dharma and artha;
for even when guarded, they are difficult to restrain, since sensual desires carry one away along that path.
The faculties of the wise, though worn by age, become reflective and intent on stability;
they turn toward tranquility with little effort, simply through necessity and shame.

And therefore, having transcended youth— which is fickle, dominated by sense objects, heedless, impatient, lacking foresight, and full of many deceits— they breathe a sigh of relief as if having crossed a wilderness.
Therefore, let this youthful age—which is unsteady, fickle, and prone to negligence—pass away for now;
for the early stage of life cannot be protected from the senses, which are the very arrows of Desire.
Moreover, if your desire is for righteousness alone, then perform a sacrifice; this is the family tradition.
For it was by presiding over sacrifices that even Indra ascended to the heights of heaven upon the back of the elephant Airāvata.
With arms adorned by golden armlets and necklaces, and with variegated crowns radiant with the light of jewel-lamps,
those royal sages attained that very state which the great seers reached through the toil of sacrifices.
Thus spoke the Lord of Magadha, who shone as he uttered words that were perfectly true, like the sun;
yet, having heard them, the prince did not waver, remaining firm like Mount Kailāsa with its many variegated peaks.
Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Visit to Śreṇya," in the *Buddhacarita*, a great poem composed by Aśvaghoṣa.

Then, having been thus addressed by the Lord of Magadha with words that were contrary to his purpose, though spoken by a friend, the son of Śuddhodana—composed, unshaken, and pure in lineage and integrity—spoke these words: *Buddhacarita* 11.1.
It is no wonder that such conduct should be yours, born as you are in the great lineage of the lion;
for this is the pure way of life for one who desires friends and acts toward his circle of friends with friendship.
Affection for the unworthy, though inherited from one's own family, does not endure among them, just as prosperity does not remain with the faint-hearted;
but the virtuous increase that very affection which was established by their ancestors through a succession of friendly acts.

Those men in this world who share the same purpose as their friends during times of hardship, I recognize them with my intellect as true friends; for who would not be a friend to one who is healthy and in a state of prosperity?
And thus, those who, having acquired wealth in this world, employ it for the sake of friends and the Dharma—
their riches, having attained their true essence, do not cause them remorse at the end when they have perished.
O King, because of your friendship and your nobility toward me, this is indeed the resolve you have formed;
out of that very friendship, I shall offer you consolation, for I would say nothing else in response to this.
Having recognized the fear of old age and death, I have sought this Dharma out of a desire for liberation;
I have abandoned my dear kinsmen with tearful faces, let alone sensual pleasures, which are the causes of misfortune.
I do not fear venomous serpents, nor indeed thunderbolts fallen from the sky,
nor fires fanned by the wind, as much as I fear the objects of the senses themselves.
For sensual desires are impermanent, thieves of one's welfare and purpose; they are empty and like illusions in this world.
Even when merely longed for, they delude the minds of men—how much more so when they are present within oneself!
For those overcome by sensual desires find no peace even in the triple heaven, much less in the world of mortals;
for there is no satisfaction for one who thirsts for desires, just as there is none for a wind-fanned fire through its fuel.
In this world, there is no misfortune equal to sensual desires, yet out of delusion people remain attached to them.
Having understood this truth, what wise person, fearing such misfortune, would of their own accord desire that which is harmful?
Even having gained the earth with its ocean-mouths, they still desire to conquer the further shore of the great sea;
there is no satiation for the world's desires, just as there is none for the ocean by the waters that fall into it.
Even after the god had rained down a shower of gold, and having conquered all four continents and even attained half of Śakra’s throne, Māndhātṛ remained unsatiated with sense objects.
Even after enjoying sovereignty over the gods in heaven when Śatakratu had vanished through fear of Vṛtra,
Nahuṣa fell, for he was insatiable in his desires and, out of pride, even made the great seers carry him.
And King Aiḍa, having entered the triple heaven and brought Queen Urvaśī under his control,
went to his destruction— insatiable in sensual pleasures— because he desired to seize gold from the ṛṣis out of greed.
Bali [attained] Mahendra from Nahuṣa, and Indra again [attained it] from Mahendra through Nahuṣa;
who could place trust in those realms, whether in heaven or on earth, which are so turbulent with the fluctuations of fortune?

Even sages who wear rags for clothing, subsist on roots, fruits, and water, and bear matted locks as long as serpents— those who have not been broken by these [sensual desires]— who then would seek out those enemies known as "desire"?

Even Ugrāyudha, though he wielded fierce weapons, met his death at the hands of Bhīṣma for their sake; even the mere thought of them brings ill fortune and leads to the destruction of those who follow virtuous conduct, so what need is there to mention those who live without vows?
Considering the taste of sense objects to be meager, their fetters to be excessive, and their lack of satisfaction to be certain,
as well as the reproach of the virtuous and inevitable sin— who would take up that poison called desire?
Having heard of the suffering of those whose souls are possessed by desire and who are oppressed by labors such as agriculture,
and having observed the composure of those who have no curiosity for sensual pleasures, it is fitting for self-possessed men to abandon desires.
One should know that misfortune lies in the desire for the fulfillment of desires; for when desires are accomplished, one falls into intoxication.
Through intoxication, one performs what ought not to be done and neglects what ought to be done, whereby, being ruined, one enters upon an evil rebirth.

Having acquired with great effort and guarded them carefully, those sensual pleasures depart once again, deceiving one; what wise person here, possessing self-mastery, would take delight in these pleasures that are like borrowed goods?
Having sought them out and grasped them, they become thirstier still; not abandoning them, they wander about in suffering.
In this world, what person of self-mastery could find delight in those sensual pleasures, which are like a torch of straw?

Whose self-possessed mind would find delight in those sensual pleasures, which are like fierce, angry serpents, and by which those who lack self-mastery, once bitten in the heart, meet with destruction and find no peace?
Like dogs tormented by hunger who remain unsatisfied even after eating,
what person of self-control could find delight in those sensual pleasures which are like the skeletons of decayed bones?

For whom, being self-possessed, could there be delight in those sensual pleasures— which, like bait cast out for fish, produce suffering because they are common property to kings, thieves, water, and fire?
For one who dwells amidst calamities on every side— from enemies as well as from kinsmen—
who that possesses self-mastery could find delight in those sensual pleasures which are like lurking predators and resemble a trap?

For what person of self-mastery could find delight in sensual pleasures— which are like fruits on the very tips of trees— that bring ruin to those who attempt to scale them, whether on a mountain, in a forest, in water, or in the ocean?

What person of self-possession could find delight in those sensual pleasures, which resemble the enjoyments of a dream, and which, though acquired through various intense efforts, go to destruction here in an instant?

Having acquired them, yet not attaining peace; having increased them, yet not preserving them—who that possesses self-mastery could find delight in those sensual pleasures which are like pits of glowing coals?
For whose sake the Kurus perished, as did the Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, and Mekhaladaṇḍakas;
what person of self-mastery could find delight in those sensual pleasures which are like the wooden blocks of a slaughterhouse?
What self-possessed person could find delight in those sensual pleasures, which cause the embrace of affection yet led the two asuras, Sunda and Upasunda, to perish through their mutual enmity?
For whose sake do people here cast their very selves into water, fire, and among carnivorous beasts—
those desires which are hostile and inauspicious? What person of self-possession could find delight in such things?
For the sake of desire, the ignorant person acts miserably and encounters suffering such as execution and imprisonment;
for the sake of desire, the wretched world of living beings, made miserable by hope, undergoes toil and meets with death.

For deer are lured to their slaughter by songs; moths fall into the fire for the sake of its form; and the fish, seeking the bait, swallows the iron hook. Therefore, sense objects result in misfortune.

As for the notion that sensual pleasures are enjoyments, when examined closely, there are no such enjoyments at all; rather, one should understand that in this world, things such as clothing—which are merely the qualities of material objects—are actually remedies for suffering.
For water is desired for the quenching of thirst, and food likewise for the destruction of hunger;
a house for protection against wind, sun, and rain; and clothing for covering the privities and warding off the cold.
Likewise, a bed is for the sake of interrupting sleep; a vehicle is for the destruction of fatigue from travel;
a seat is for the purpose of changing one's position; and bathing is for the sake of cleanliness, health, and strength.
Therefore, objects are not enjoyments for living beings, but rather means for the alleviation of suffering.
What wise person, engaged in the practice of remedial measures, would accept the notion that "I am enjoying pleasures"?

He who, being scorched by the burning heat of bile, should determine that the application of cold measures is an enjoyment, and who, engaged in the method of counteracting suffering, should apply the designation "enjoyment" to sensual pleasures—[he alone would be justified]. (Bc 11.40)
And because sensual pleasures are uncertain, for that reason as well I have no notion of them as enjoyments;
for those very things that bestow happiness bring about suffering once again.
Heavy garments and aloe-wood are indeed for comfort in the cold, but for discomfort in the heat;
the rays of the moon and sandalwood are for comfort in the heat, but become sources of suffering in the cold.
Since in this world all people are beset by pairs of opposites, such as loss and gain and so forth,
for this reason too there is no one on earth who is exclusively happy, nor anyone who is exclusively miserable.
Having seen that pleasure and pain are intermingled, I consider sovereignty and servitude to be equal;
for a king does not always laugh, nor indeed is a slave always in distress.
Since authority is considered superior in kingship, it is for this very reason that the sufferings of a king are great;
for a king, resembling a wooden puppet, undergoes exhaustion for the sake of the world.
If a king places his trust in a kingdom that is devoid of generosity and full of many enemies, he meets with ruin;
yet, even if he attains confidence therein, what indeed is the happiness for a king who remains ever-trembling?
And when, even after conquering the entire earth, only a single city is seen fit for residence,
and within that, only a single dwelling is to be occupied— is not the status of a king, then, merely toil for the sake of others?
For the king as well, there was but a single pair of garments; likewise, a mere measure of food for the sake of suppressing hunger;
and similarly, a single bed and a single seat—any further luxuries were only for the intoxication of the monarch.
And if this fruit is desired for the sake of contentment, then even without a kingdom I have contentment;
for when a person possesses contentment in this world, are not all distinctions indeed without distinction?
Therefore, I am not to be enticed back toward sensual desires, for I have set out upon the secure and auspicious path;
yet, remembering our friendship, speak to me again and again, saying, "Surely, you must fulfill your vow."
For it is not out of resentment that I have entered the forest, nor because my head has been struck by the arrows of an enemy;
nor is it because I have a longing for fruits superior to these that I do not accept this speech of yours.

He who, having released a furious, venomous serpent, would resolve to seize it again, or who, having cast away a burning grass-torch that consumes by its heat, would pursue sensual desires once more—[he alone would be such]. (Bc 11.52)
He who is sighted might envy the blind, the liberated the bound, the wealthy the destitute, and he of sound mind the mad; yet he would envy one whose soul is devoted to the objects of the senses.
One who subsists on alms is not to be pitied, for he is a man of accomplishment seeking to cross over the fear of old age and death;
he possesses here the supreme bliss of peace, and for him, sufferings in the next world are brought to an end.
Even while abiding in great prosperity, one who is overwhelmed by craving is to be pitied—
he who does not attain the bliss of peace in this world and is seized by sufferings in the next.
"It is indeed worthy of your character, conduct, and lineage to speak thus;
it is likewise fitting for me to fulfill my vow, in accordance with my own character, conduct, and lineage."
For I, pierced by the arrow of saṃsāra and having fled from it, desire to attain peace;
I would not wish to obtain even a flawless kingdom in the third heaven, much less among human beings.

"O King, as for what you have told me—that the complete pursuit of the three aims of life (trivarga) is the supreme goal of man—I see it here as nothing but a misfortune; for the three aims are perishable and do not bring true satisfaction. (Buddhacarita 11.58)
But that state in which there is neither old age, nor fear, nor disease, nor birth, nor even cessation, nor mental afflictions—
that alone I consider the supreme human goal, wherein action does not recur again and again.

As for what you said—that old age should be awaited because youth undergoes transformation—this is uncertain, for it is seen to be fickle; indeed, old age can be lacking in fortitude, while youth can possess steadfastness.

And since Death, expert in his own work, drags the world helplessly through all stages of life, how can a wise man seeking peace wait for old age when the time of destruction is so unstable? (Bc 11.61)
When Death stands like an inauspicious hunter, with old age as his bow and diseases scattered as his arrows,
