striking down the deer of living beings that dwell in the forest of fortune— what hope can there be for the prolongation of life?

Therefore, whether one is young, old, or even a child, one ought to act here with such haste that the conduct of a righteous person— one who has perfected the self— may result either in active engagement or in renunciation.

And as for what you said—that I should perform sacrificial rites for the sake of dharma, which yield desired fruits and are appropriate for my lineage—I pay homage to such sacrifices; indeed, I do not desire happiness that is sought by inflicting suffering upon another.
Indeed, for one who is compassionate by nature, it is not fitting to kill another who is helpless out of a desire for the fruit [of sacrifice];
even if the fruit of such a rite were eternal, how much less so when it consists of destruction? (Bc 11.65)
Even if there were no other way for dharma to exist than through vows, moral conduct, or the tranquility of mind,
one still ought not to perform a sacrifice in which the highest fruit is said to consist in the slaughter of another being.

Even in this life, the pleasure that arises for a person remaining here through the harming of others is undesirable to the compassionate and wise man; what then need be said of that which is not seen in future lives?
And I am not to be enticed toward the pursuit of fruits; O King, my mind finds no delight in worldly existences.
For all worldly activities are as fickle as creepers struck by the rain from a cloud, for they are unstable in every respect.

Having come here from that place out of a desire to see the sage Arāḍa, who teaches liberation, I shall depart this very day, O King; may you be well, and forgive my words which are harsh due to their concern for the truth.

O King, protect us like Indra in heaven; protect us constantly like the sun with your virtues; protect our welfare here, protect the earth, protect our life, protect us through the noble, protect our virtuous sons, protect our fortunes, and protect your own dharma.
Just as a bird, in the interval between the birth and death of the one whose banner is fire, flies away casting off its body;
so too, in this interval—the destruction of the enemy who is the foe of snow—fly forth, casting off the mind.
With palms joined in reverence and his desire fulfilled, the king said: "May you obtain whatever you wish without hindrance;
and when you have achieved this fulfillment of your purpose in due time, you must likewise show me your favor."
Having firmly promised "so be it" to the king, he then departed for the hermitage of Vaiśvamtara;
and beholding him departing as a wandering mendicant, the king was filled with wonder and returned to the city of Girivraja.
Thus ends the eleventh canto, titled "The Censure of Desire," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.
Then the moon of the Ikṣvāku dynasty, filling [the space] as it were with his physical form, approached the hermitage of Araḍa, the sage who dwells in tranquility.
Having been addressed with a loud "Welcome! by that man of the Kālāma clan even from afar as soon as he was seen, he drew near.
Having mutually inquired according to propriety about each other's physical well-being,
the two sat down on a pure spot upon two wooden seats that were sacred, strengthening, and auspicious.
To that prince as he sat there, that best of sages spoke,
as if drinking him in with his two large eyes full of great respect.
It is known to me, O gentle one, how you departed from your home,
having severed the bond of affection like a proud elephant breaking its tether.
In every respect, your mind is indeed steadfast and wise,
since you have come here having abandoned royal fortune like a creeper bearing poisonous fruit.
It is no wonder that kings of advanced age retired to the forest after bestowing their royal splendor upon their offspring, like a garland already worn out and discarded.
This thought of mine is a marvel: that you, while still in the bloom of youth, have reached this state without having enjoyed royal splendor, yet remain within the range of sensory objects.
To understand this supreme Dharma, you are the worthy vessel;
taking hold of the raft of knowledge, cross swiftly over the ocean of suffering.
"Although a treatise is expounded over time once a disciple has been tested,
you need not be examined by me, because of your profundity and your resolve."
Having understood these words of Ārāḍa, that bull among men became exceedingly pleased and spoke this reply: Bc_12.11 //
That this supreme benevolence of yours exists even toward one who is dispassionate—
by this, though I have not yet accomplished my goal, I now feel as if I have achieved it.
For I consider the sight of you to be like one desiring to see light, like one wishing to travel seeking a guide, and like one wishing to cross over seeking a boat.
Therefore, if you think it should be spoken, please tell me that which must be said,
so that he may be completely liberated from old age, death, and disease.
Thus impelled by the very majesty of the prince,
Ārāḍa succinctly declared the definitive conclusion of his own teaching.
O best of listeners, hear this our established doctrine:
how saṃsāra comes to be and how it indeed ceases.
Nature and its transformations, as well as birth, death, and old age—these are called existence (sattva); O you of steadfast being, go beyond that.
In this regard, O you who are skilled in the nature of things, know that what is called "nature" consists of the five elements, the ego-sense, the intellect, and the unmanifest itself.
Understand that the sense objects and the sense organs are transformations;
likewise, the hands, feet, speech, the anus, the genitals, and the mind are transformations.
From the knowledge of this field, it is designated as the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña);
and those who contemplate the self refer to the self as the "knower of the field. (Bc 12.20)
It is recorded in tradition that Kapila, together with his disciples, was awakened here;
whereas Prajāpati, along with his son, is said to be unawakened here.
That which is born, decays, is afflicted, and dies should be known as the manifest; the unmanifest, however, is the opposite.
Ignorance, karma, and craving are to be known as the causes of saṃsāra;
while a living being remains within this triad, it does not transcend its state of existence.
From misconception, from egoism, from doubt, from confusion, from lack of distinction, from lack of means, from attachment, and from falling away.
In that context, what is called "misconception" (vipratyaya) functions erroneously; it performs a task in one way, yet conceives of it as being otherwise.
"I speak, I know, I go, I stand"—
thus does the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) function here, O you who are free from ego-sense.
But he who perceives entities as undifferentiated and without doubt, like a lump of clay, is here called "doubtless" (asaṃdeha), though he is actually in doubt. (Bc 12.27)
"That which is I am this very mind, intellect, and action;
that which is this collection [of factors] is I"—this is what is called "complete immersion" (abhisaṃplava).
O Knower of Distinctions, he who understands the lack of distinction between the awakened and the unawakened,
as well as among the constituent natures (prakṛtis), is remembered as "the Undifferentiated" (aviśeṣa).
O you who know the means, the wise have declared that acts such as salutations, the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, sprinkling, and ritual ablutions are not the means [to liberation].
That by which the dull-witted person becomes attached through mind, speech, intellect,
and action toward sense objects— that lack of attachment is known as non-attachment (anabhiṣvaṅga).
That suffering which one conceives as "this is mine" or "I am this" is to be known as the downfall by which one is cast down into saṃsāra.
Thus, knowing ignorance, he strives against its five stages:
darkness, delusion, great delusion, and the two types of gloom.
In this regard, know that indolence is *tamas*, and delusion is both death and birth;
but let it be understood, O free from delusion, that great delusion (*mahāmoha*) is simply desire.
Because even great beings become utterly deluded herein,
therefore, O mighty-armed one, this is known as "Great Delusion" (mahāmoha).
O Akrodha, they designate anger itself as *tāmisra*;
and they declare despondency to be *andhatāmisra*, while the absence of despondency is called *pradīpa*.
Joined with this ignorance consisting of five parts, the fool is drenched in births within saṃsāra, which abounds in suffering. (Bc 12.37)
The seer, the hearer, the thinker, and the very performer of actions—
having come to identify with these as "I," one revolves in saṃsāra.
O wise one, by these causes the stream of birth proceeds here;
you should understand that in the absence of the cause, there is an absence of the fruit.
In this regard, one who desires liberation should understand with right understanding these four:
the awakened and the unawakened, as well as the manifest and the unmanifest.
Having understood these four as they truly are, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña),
having abandoned the state of coming and going, attains the imperishable state.
For this reason, the Brahmins in the world, who are exponents of the supreme Brahman,
practice celibacy here and cause other Brahmins to dwell [in that state].
Having heard these words of the sage, the prince asked about the means [to liberation] as well as the ultimate state.
"You ought to explain this practice of the holy life— how it is to be practiced, to what extent, and where— and also the ultimate limit of this Dharma."
Then Ārāḍa, in accordance with the scriptures, explained that very Dharma to him again in another manner, concisely and with its meaning made perfectly clear.
Having first abandoned his home and adopted the mark of a mendicant,
he lives having taken up the morality that is extensive through right conduct.
Relying upon supreme contentment, wherever he may be and by whatever means,
the skillful knower of the scriptures, free from the pairs of opposites, frequents a solitary dwelling.
Then, seeing fear in passion and supreme auspiciousness in dispassion,
he restrains the collection of his senses and strives for the tranquility of the mind.
Then, secluded from sensual desires and from ill-will and the like,
he attains the first dhyāna, born of seclusion and accompanied by applied thought (vitarka).
Having attained that very bliss of meditative absorption, the foolish person is carried away by the thought of it, thinking, "I have gained a bliss never before experienced. (Bc 12.50)
By such tranquility as this, which loathes desire and hatred,
one attains the world of Brahmā, being deceived by superficial contentment.
Having understood that discursive thoughts cause agitation of the mind,
the wise man attains a meditative absorption free from them, accompanied by joy and bliss.
He who, being carried away by that affection, does not perceive any distinction,
attains a radiant station among the Ābhāsvara gods.
But he who withdraws the mind from that joy and bliss attains the third dhyāna, a bliss devoid of joy.
But he who is immersed in that bliss and makes no effort for further distinction attains a commonality of happiness with the Śubhakṛtsna deities.
Having attained such pleasure, he who does not become attached but remains equanimous attains the fourth dhyāna, which is devoid of both pleasure and pain.
In that regard, some who are conceitedly convinced resolve that liberation consists in the abandonment of pleasure and pain, as well as the non-activity of the mind. (Bc 12.57)
However, those who examine with great wisdom declare that the fruit of this meditation is equal to that of the gods of the Bṛhatphala heaven, lasting for a vast duration of time.
Having emerged from that meditative concentration and having seen the defects of embodied beings,
the wise man ascends to knowledge for the sake of turning away from the body.
Then, having abandoned that meditation and made a firm resolve regarding the ultimate distinction,
the wise one becomes detached even from form, just as he was from sensual desires.
First imagining the cavities within this body,
one then resolves upon space even within solid substances.
But another wise person, having contracted the self that had gone into space and beholding that very same [self] as infinite, attains excellence.
But another, skilled in inner practice, having turned back the self by means of the self and perceiving that "nothing exists," is known as one who dwells in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanya*).
Then, like a blade of grass from a muñja reed or a bird from a cage,
the *kṣetrajña* having emerged from the body is designated as "liberated."
This is that supreme Brahman, signless, eternal, and imperishable,
which the wise who know reality call "liberation."
Thus have both the means and liberation been shown to you by me;
if you understand them and find them pleasing, practice them accordingly.
Jaigīṣavya, Janaka, the aged Parāśara,
and others who sought liberation, having followed this path, were indeed liberated.
Having thus received his words and reflected upon them, he,
empowered by the force of his previous causes, spoke this reply.
"I have heard this subtle knowledge, which is auspicious in its successive stages;
yet, because the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) has not been relinquished, I understand this to be non-final."
For I consider the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), even when liberated from the primary causes and their transformations,
to still possess the nature of procreation and the nature of a seed.
Even if the self is conceived as pure and liberated, it will again become unliberated due to the continued existence of causal conditions.
Just as a seed does not sprout due to the absence of season, soil, and water, so too, in my view, that [embryo] likewise fails to develop in the absence of those various conditions.
Since liberation is conceived as resulting from the abandonment of karma, ignorance, and craving,
such absolute abandonment is not possible if a self exists.
Having abandoned and abandoned these three, a distinction is indeed perceived;
yet wherever the self remains, there these three remain subtle.
Furthermore, because the faults are subtle, because the mind is inactive,
and because the lifespan is long, liberation is indeed postulated.
This abandonment of egoism that is being conceptualized is actually the abandonment of the self;
there is no abandonment of egoism [possible] as long as the self exists.
Furthermore, one who is not liberated from number and the like cannot be devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).
Therefore, in the absence of the state of being devoid of qualities, liberation is not predicated for him.
For there is no separation between the possessor of qualities and the qualities themselves;
indeed, fire is never perceived apart from its form and heat.
Before the body there would be no embodied being, and likewise before the qualities there would be no possessor of qualities;
therefore, having been liberated at the outset, the embodied one is bound again.
The knower of the field (kṣetrajña), being devoid of a body, must be either a knower or indeed a non-knower.
If he is a knower, there exists for him an object of knowledge; and as long as there is an object of knowledge, he is not liberated.
Then, if [the self] is "ignorant," what is the use of this imagined self for you?
For even without a self, ignorance is well-established, as in the case of wood or a wall.
Since renunciation is considered virtuous only when it proceeds further and further,
I believe that through the total relinquishment of everything, one achieves complete fulfillment of purpose.
Having understood this teaching of Arāḍa to be incomplete, he was not satisfied;
realizing it was insufficient, he then departed from there.
Then, desiring to hear about his specific teachings, he went to Udraka’s hermitage;
yet, because of Udraka's grasping at a self, he did not accept his philosophical view.
Having understood the fault in both perception and non-perception, the sage Udraka attained the state beyond the realm of nothingness, which consists of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Because perception and non-perception are subtle with respect to their object,
and beyond that there is neither perception nor non-perception, therefore one should aspire to reach that state.
And because the intellect remains fixed right there, without wandering elsewhere,
being subtle and unsharp, therefore in that state there is neither non-perception nor perception.
And because even having attained that, the world returns once more,
the Bodhisattva, desiring the supreme [state], abandoned Udraka.
Then, having left that hermitage, he who was seeking the highest good and had made his resolve proceeded to the hermitage known as the city of the royal seer Gaya.
Then, on the pure bank of the Nairañjanā, the sage of pure prowess,
delighting in solitary dwelling, made his abode.
There he beheld five monks who had arrived, who were practitioners of vows engaged in asceticism, having previously been overcome by the agitation of the five senses.
And having seen him there, O monks, those seekers of liberation stood before him,
as people drawn by the objects of the senses stand before a lord who possesses wealth and health acquired through merit.
He was being honored by those eminent disciples who followed him with humility and remained under his control, just as the restless senses follow the mind.
Thinking, "This may be the means for bringing an end to birth and death," he then undertook difficult austerities, beginning with fasting.
Performing many rules for fasting that are difficult for men to practice,
he brought about emaciation of his own body for six years, desiring tranquility.
And at meal times, desiring to reach the further shore of the shoreless cycle of existence, he sustained himself with only one of each— millet, sesame, and rice.
Whatever emaciation was produced in his body by that asceticism,
that very same thing was subsequently turned into an increase of his vital splendor.
Though emaciated, he possessed the glory of vast renown and brought joy to the eyes of others,
just as the autumn moon at the beginning of its bright fortnight brings delight to the night-lotuses.
Though reduced to skin and bone, with his fat, flesh, and blood entirely exhausted,
he shone like the ocean, whose depth remains undiminished even when it is diminished.
Then the sage, his body clearly emaciated by arduous austerities and distressed in vain, fearing worldly existence and desiring Buddhahood, formed this resolve: *Bodhicaryāvatāra* 12.100.
This dharma does not lead to dispassion, nor to awakening, nor to liberation;
that method which was attained by me at the foot of the Jambu tree remains constant.
Realizing that this could not be attained by one who was weak, he developed a sense of urgency;
for the sake of increasing his physical strength, he reflected further on this matter.
Exhausted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, and with a mind unsteady due to weariness,
how could one who lacks inner peace attain the fruit that is to be realized by the mind?
Nirvāṇa is correctly attained through the constant gratification of the sense faculties;
by means of having the sense faculties fully gratified, one attains mental well-being.
For one whose mind is healthy and serene, meditative absorption (samādhi) arises;
for one whose mind is endowed with meditative absorption, the practice of meditation (dhyāna-yoga) proceeds.
Through the practice of meditation, those dharmas are attained by which that supreme,
immortal state— peaceful, ageless, and difficult to reach— is obtained.
Therefore, he reached the certainty that this means is rooted in food;
thus, the steadfast one of immeasurable intellect resolved to take food.
Having bathed, he, emaciated, slowly ascended from the bank of the Nairañjanā River,
as the trees on the shore, their branch-tips bent down through devotion, offered him a hand.
Then Nandabalā, the daughter of the lord of cowherds, impelled by the deities,
arrived there with her heart overflowing with joy.
With her arms radiant with white conch shells and wearing a dark blue woolen garment,
she was like the Yamunā, the best of rivers, whose waters are dark blue and garlanded with foam.
Her joy increased by faith, with her lotus-eyes blossoming,
she prostrated herself before him with her head and caused him to accept the milk-rice.
Having enjoyed it and thereby attained the fruit of his birth,
he became capable of reaching awakening, with his six sense-faculties fully satisfied.
With his form fully nourished and accompanied by his own glory, the Sage alone bore the loveliness and steadfastness of both the moon and the ocean.
Perceiving that he had turned back, the five mendicants abandoned him,
just as the five elements abandon the wise man when he has attained liberation.
Then, accompanied by his resolve, he who had made a firm determination for enlightenment proceeded to the foot of an *aśvattha* tree, where the ground was covered with young grass.

Then, at that time, the supreme serpent Kāla, whose prowess was like that of a lordly elephant, being awakened by the incomparable sound of the Great Sage’s footsteps and certain of his arrival for enlightenment, spoke this hymn of praise.
O Sage, since the earth seems to groan again and again as it is pressed down by your feet,
and since your radiance shines like the sun, you will surely enjoy your desired fruit this very day.
Just as rows of blue jays wheeling in the sky circumambulate you clockwise, O lotus-eyed one,
and just as gentle breezes blow in the heavens, today you will certainly become a Buddha.
Then, having been praised by the foremost of serpents, he who had made his vow took pure grass from the reaper and sat down for the sake of awakening at the foot of a pure, great tree.
Then he assumed an unsurpassed, unshakable cross-legged posture, coiled like the body of a sleeping serpent, thinking:
"I shall not break this seat upon the earth until I have attained my goal."
Then the gods attained incomparable joy; the herds of deer did not cry out, nor did the birds;
and the forest trees did not rustle when struck by the wind, for the Blessed One had fixed his mind upon his firm resolve while seated.
Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Visit to Ārāḍa," in the great epic poem *Buddhacarita*.
When that great seer, born of a lineage of royal sages, had sat down there having made his vow for liberation, the world rejoiced, but Māra, the enemy of the True Dharma, trembled with fear.
Him whom they call Kāmadeva in the world, who possesses variegated weapons and flower-arrows,
and who is the sovereign lord of the movement of desire— it is he alone whom they declare to be Māra, the enemy of liberation.
His three sons—Vibhrama, Harṣa, and Darpa—and his three daughters—Arati, Prīti, and Tṛṣā—questioned him regarding the transformation of the mind; and he spoke these words to them all.
That sage, wearing the armor of resolve, drawing back the arrow of wisdom with the weapon of courage, sits desiring to conquer my sense-objects; therefore, this is the sorrow of my mind.
For if he should surpass me and depart, proclaiming the path to liberation to the world,
then this realm of mine will today become empty, like that of the King of Videha when he fell from his conduct.
Therefore, while he still stands within my domain and has not yet attained the eye of wisdom,
I shall go to break his vow, just as the swollen current of a river breaks a dam.
Then, taking up a bow made of flowers and five arrows that delude the world,
he approached the foot of the Ashvattha tree with his son, bringing unease to the minds of all living beings.

Then Māra, having fixed his left hand upon the tip of his weapon and playing with an arrow, spoke thus to the tranquil Sage who sat upon his seat, desiring to cross to the further shore of the ocean of existence: Bc_13.8 //
"Arise, O Kṣatriya! You who fear death, practice your own duty; abandon the dharma of liberation.
By subduing the world with arrows and sacrifices, attain the station of Vāsava from this world."
For this path is glorious for one to depart upon, which was trodden by the most ancient lords of men;
it is not fitting for one born in the vast lineage of royal seers to resort to this ignoble life of begging.
Therefore, O firm-minded one, if you do not rise today, remain steadfast and do not abandon your vow;
for this very arrow is raised by me, the same one that was released against Śūrpaka, the enemy of the fish.

Even Aiḍa, the grandson of Soma, became distraught when touched by this [disease] in some way; and Śantanu likewise lost his self-control. When the age has declined, what need be said of any other weakling?

Therefore, rise quickly and regain your senses; for here stands this arrow, licking its lips, which I shall not release against those who are obedient to their beloveds and dear to Rati, even as I do not discharge it at the cakravāka birds.
Even when addressed in this way, Śākyamuni, being free from desire, did not shift his seat at all;
then Māra discharged an arrow at him, having placed his daughters and sons before him.
But even when that arrow was released, he paid it no heed and did not waver from his steadfastness;
seeing him thus, Māra despaired and, overcome with anxiety, spoke softly: Bc_13.15.
He does not even think of that very arrow by which the Lord Śambhu himself was pierced and shaken when aimed at the Daughter of the Mountain King;
could it be that this arrow is mindless? No, it is not so.
Therefore, he does not deserve the flower-arrowed god, nor exhilaration, nor even the service of Rati;
he deserves instead to be terrified, threatened, and beaten by hosts of ungentle spirits.
Then Māra, desiring to create an obstacle to the pacification of Śākyamuni, recalled his own army;
and his followers, devoid of refuge, surrounded him with trees, spears, clubs, maces, and swords in their hands.
Some had the faces of boars, fish, horses, donkeys, and camels; others had the faces of tigers, bears, lions, and elephants;
some were one-eyed, some had many mouths, some had three heads, some had pendulous bellies, and others had protruding navels.
Some were without knees or thighs, some had knees like jars, some were armed with fangs, and others with claws;
some had skulls for faces, some possessed many forms, some had broken or half-faces, and others had enormous mouths.
Tawny with ashes, variegated with red spots, carrying skull-topped staffs in their hands, with hair as greenish-grey as smoke,
wearing long garlands and ears hanging like those of elephants, they were clad in skins or else entirely naked.
Some had white faces and green bodies, others were copper-colored, smoky, tawny, or black;
their arms were draped with snake-skins as upper garments, and they wore girdles cluttered with loudly ringing bells.

Some were as tall as palm trees, grasping spears; others were as small as children, with fangs bared in a terrifying snarl; some had the faces of sheep but the eyes of birds; and others had the faces of cats but the bodies of humans.
With disheveled hair, some with topknots, others half-shaven, clad in red garments and with turbans in disarray;
with faces beaming with joy yet frowning at times, they were both captivating and draining away one's vital energy.
Some, as they went along, leaped about violently; others likewise sprang at one another;
some sported while moving through the air, and others moved about upon the tops of trees.
One danced while whirling his trident; another roared, dragging his mace with a thunderous crash;
one bellowed with joy like a bull; and another blazed forth from the hairs of his body.
Such hosts of spirits stood surrounding the foot of that Bodhi tree on all sides,
both desiring to seize him and desiring to strike him, while fulfilling the command of their lord.
Beholding that time of battle between Māra and the Bull of the Śākyas during the first watch of the night,
the sky did not shine, the earth trembled, and the quarters of the horizon blazed forth with sound.
The wind blew in every direction with increased force; the stars did not shimmer and the moon did not shine;
the night spread forth even greater darkness, and all the oceans were thoroughly agitated.
The mountain-like elephants, devoted to righteousness and unable to endure the obstacle placed before the Great Sage,
hissed and yawned with eyes wide open in rage toward Māra.

But the eminent gods, pure and dwelling in the higher realms, having set out for the sake of the accomplishment of the True Dharma, felt compassion for Māra in their minds; yet, because they were free from passion, they did not succumb to anger.

Beholding that foot of the Bodhi tree strewn with that army of Māra, whose nature is violence, those whose very soul is the Dharma and who desire the liberation of the world raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! in the sky.
Seeing that host of Māra standing there as an obstacle to his practice of Dharma,
the great seer was neither agitated nor did he undergo any change of state, like a lion seated in the midst of cattle.
Then Māra commanded his surging host of spirits for the sake of terrifying him;
thereupon, that army, by means of their respective powers, set its mind upon breaking his fortitude.

Some stood there, indeed, terrifying all beings: their tongues flickering and hanging out at various lengths, their sharp-pointed fangs bared, their eyes like the orbs of the sun, their mouths agape, and their ears fixed like spikes.
Though they stood there, so formidable in both appearance and disposition,
the great seer was neither shaken nor terrified by them, as if they were merely unruly children at play.
Then one man, his eyes rolling with rage, raised a mace against him;
yet his arm, together with the mace, became paralyzed, like the arm of Puraṃdara in the city of Tripura when he raised his thunderbolt.
Some, having raised up rocks and trees, were unable at all to hurl them at the Sage;
they fell down just so, with their trees and rocks, like the foothills of the Vindhya mountains shattered by a thunderbolt.
Some, leaping up into the sky, hurled rocks, trees, and battle-axes;
yet they remained suspended in the air as if paralyzed, failing to descend like the multicolored rays of twilight clouds.
Another hurled at him a blazing bundle of straw as large as a mountain peak;
yet, by his power, it shattered into a hundred pieces while still remaining in the sky as soon as it was released.
Like the blazing sun risen in the sky, one [being] discharged a great rain of glowing coals;
like Mount Meru ablaze at the end of an eon, he scattered the dust from the hollows of golden mountains.
But that rain of glowing coals, accompanied by sparks, as it was being scattered at the foot of the Bodhi tree,
became a rain of red lotus petals due to the supreme ṛṣi’s dwelling in loving-kindness.
Though his body and mind were tormented by such miseries and he was being struck down by those very things,
Śākyamuni did not stir from his seat, embracing his own resolve as if it were a kinsman.
Then others disgorged serpents from their mouths, as if from withered trees;
bound by his spells, they could not hiss, nor slither, nor move in his presence.
Then other massive clouds appeared, accompanied by lightning and the fierce roar of thunder;
they released a shower of stones upon that tree, which instead became a beautiful rain of flowers.
Then, when an arrow was placed upon the bow by another, it blazed right there and did not fly forth;
like the wrath of an impatient man who is powerless over himself when it is being stirred up.
But five arrows, released by another, remained suspended in the sky and did not fall upon the sage,
like the five sense-faculties of an investigator who fears cyclic existence when they encounter the objects of the senses.
Another, enraged and desiring to strike, rushed forward toward the great seer wielding a mace;
failing to reach his goal, he fell helpless, just as people fall into harmful vices that bring only misfortune.

A woman named Meghakālī, however, carrying a skull in her hand, wandered there restlessly to bewilder the mind of the great seer; she did not remain still, like the intellect of a fickle person regarding the sacred scriptures.
A certain man, his eyes inflamed as if wishing to burn with the fire of his gaze like a venomous serpent,
beheld the Seer seated right there— though he was possessed by desire— as if he were the very teaching of the highest good.
Likewise, another, lifting a heavy rock, labored in vain with his efforts frustrated,
like one desiring to attain the Dharma— which is reached through knowledge and meditative concentration and leads to the supreme good— by means of physical exhaustion.
Others, with the forms of hyenas and lions, let out great, loud roars;
at which all creatures fled in every direction, thinking that the sky, struck by a thunderbolt, was bursting asunder.
Deer and elephants fled and hid themselves, uttering cries of distress;
and during that night, birds flew about from all directions, crying out as if it were day, overcome with grief.
Although all living beings were shaken by those various cries of theirs,
the Sage neither trembled nor recoiled there, just as Garuḍa is unafraid of the screeching of crows.
The more the Sage did not fear the terrifying hosts of the assembly,
the more Māra, the enemy of those who uphold the Dharma, sank down under the weight of both grief and rage.

Then, a certain being of visible form, a distinguished spirit dwelling in the sky, spoke with a great voice to Māra—who had seen the rain and was free from anger—saying: *The rain has fallen; the milk is untroubled.* (Buddhacarita 13.56)
O Māra, you ought not to labor in vain; abandon your murderous nature and go to find peace.
For he cannot be shaken by you, any more than the great mountain Meru can be moved by the wind.
Fire might even abandon its nature of heat, water its fluidity, and earth its solidity;
yet he, who has accumulated meritorious karma over many eons, would never abandon his resolve.
For his resolve, his valor, his splendor, and his compassion for living beings—
without attaining the ultimate truth, he will not rise up, just as the thousand-rayed sun does not cease its course until it has destroyed the darkness.
For by rubbing wood one obtains fire, and by digging the earth one finds water;
for the persistent, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished—provided it is undertaken with justice and all things are performed correctly.
Feeling compassion for that world suffering from diseases such as passion and the like, he thought:
"This great physician, who is exerting himself for the sake of the medicine of knowledge, ought not to suffer any obstacle."

When the world has been led astray by many wrong paths, it is not fitting to disturb that guide who seeks the true path with such toil— just as one would not disturb a good guide when a caravan has lost its way.
While beings have fallen into great darkness, this lamp of wisdom is being lit;
it is not right for you, O Noble One, to extinguish it, just as it is improper to blow out a lamp that has been lit in the midst of gloom.

And seeing the world submerged in the great flood of saṃsāra, unable to find the further shore, if anyone were to harbor ill will toward him who has set out to rescue it, that person would be ignoble. (Bc 13.64)

The tree of wisdom, which bestows the fruit of Dharma—having patience for its roots, firmness for its deep-set base, conduct for its flowers, and mindfulness and intelligence for its branches—is growing; it truly does not deserve to be uprooted.

It is not fitting for you to desire to harm him whose mind is intent on liberating from the firm snares of delusion those beings who are bound therein— he who is exhausted by his efforts for the sake of releasing the world from its fetters.
For today is the fixed time for those deeds which he has performed for the sake of awakening;
it is fitting that he sits here in this very manner, just as the sages of old did.
For this is the navel of the earth’s surface, endowed with the entirety of supreme splendor;
indeed, there is no other region on earth that could withstand the force of his meditative concentration.
Therefore, do not grieve; attain peace. O Māra, let there be no pride in you because of your greatness.
It is not fit to place trust in fortune that is as unstable as honey; why do you indulge in astonishment at such a shifting state?
Then, having heard those words of the great sage and having observed his unshakable steadfastness,
Māra departed dejected, his efforts frustrated— he by whose arrows the world is struck in its very heart.
Then his army fled in all directions, its joy vanished and its labor rendered fruitless, with its stones, brushwood, and trees cast aside; like an enemy host whose refuge has been destroyed by a foe.
When the Flower-Armed One (Kāmadeva) had been defeated along with his retinue, and the Great Sage, free from passion and having conquered all enemies, was victorious;
then the sky, together with the moon, shone like a young woman smiling, and a fragrant rain of flowers fell from the clouds.
Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Victory over Māra," in the *Buddhacarita*, a great poem composed by Aśvaghoṣa.
Then, having conquered the host of Māra through both fortitude and tranquility,
he who was skilled in meditation, desiring to know the ultimate truth, entered into deep reflection.
Having attained supreme mastery over all the methods of meditative concentration,
he recalled the succession of his previous births during the first watch of the night.
"In that place I was named so-and-so; having passed away from there, I have come here"—thus he recalled thousands of births as if experiencing them anew.
Recalling birth and death throughout those various rebirths, he,
whose very nature was compassion, then felt compassion for sentient beings.
Having abandoned one's own kin here and performed rites elsewhere,
this world indeed wanders like a wheel, utterly without protection.
As he was thus recollecting this, his mind became self-restrained,
and he reached the certainty that "saṃsāra is as devoid of essence as the core of a plantain tree."
When the second watch had arrived, he of peerless prowess,
the best among all who possess vision, obtained the supreme divine eye.
Then, with that divine and perfectly purified eye,
he beheld the entire world as if in a stainless mirror.
As he beheld the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their inferior and superior karma, his compassionate nature increased.
"These living beings of evil deeds go to the miserable states;
these others of virtuous deeds are established in the triple heaven."
Having been reborn in this most terrifying and exceedingly cruel hell,
alas, these beings are piteously tormented by manifold sufferings.
Some are made to drink molten iron as hot as fire;
others, screaming, are impaled upon glowing-hot iron pillars.
Some are cooked like flour in iron cauldrons with their faces turned downward;
others are piteously burned in blazing heaps of glowing coals.
Some are devoured by fierce dogs with sharp iron fangs;
others are attacked by ravenous iron-beaked crows, as if made of steel.
Some, exhausted by the heat and longing for cool shade,
enter the dark forest of sword-leaves as if they were bound there.
Some, with their arms bound, are split like wood with axes;
yet even in such suffering they do not perish, for their life-breaths are sustained by their karma.
Whatever action was performed for the sake of ending suffering with the thought, "May there be happiness," its fruit is now being experienced as nothing but suffering by those who are powerless.
For those who, having committed unwholesome deeds for the sake of happiness, now suffer intensely—
does that enjoyment of theirs bring even the slightest bit of happiness?
The defiled karma that was committed with laughter by those of defiled mind is experienced with wailing when the time for its ripening arrives.
If those who have committed evil deeds were to see the fruit of their actions,
they would vomit hot blood as if struck in their vital organs.
These other wretched beings have been born into the various animal realms due to diverse karmas arising from the flickerings of the mind.
Where, for the sake of flesh, skin, hair, or teeth, and even out of enmity or intoxication, people are slaughtered piteously while their own kinsmen look on.
Though unable and helpless, tormented by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, they are made to carry burdens as oxen and horses, their bodies wounded by the goad.
And even those who have become mighty elephants are driven by the weak, their heads tormented by iron hooks and beaten with feet and heels. (Bc 14.24)
Even though other sufferings exist, there is suffering here in particular because of mutual conflict and because of total dependence on others.
Those dwelling in the sky are indeed oppressed by those who dwell in the sky; those dwelling in the water by those who move in the water;
and those dwelling on land by those situated on land—each being overcome by the others.
Likewise, those whose minds are overcome by stinginess have been reborn in the world of the ancestors,
which is devoid of light, where they experience their fruit with misery.
With mouths like the eye of a needle and bellies like mountains,
those who share in suffering are tormented by the pains born of hunger and thirst.
Transgressing their intentions yet sustained by their own past deeds,
these beings are unable to consume even the filth that has been cast away.
If a person were to know such a fruit of stinginess,
they would give away even their own limbs in every way, just like Śibi.
These other beings, born among humans in this impure pool known as the womb— which resembles hell— suffer misery.
